concepts.name: Log loss
concepts.summary: The average negative log of the probability a model gave to the true label. Confident correct predictions cost little and confident wrong ones cost a lot.
concepts.body:
For binary labels, log loss = −(1/N) Σ [y ln p + (1 − y) ln(1 − p)], where p is the predicted probability of the positive class. A perfect model scores 0, and there is no upper limit.

The penalty grows fast as a wrong prediction gets more confident. Giving the true class 0.9 costs −ln 0.9 ≈ 0.11. Giving it 0.01 costs −ln 0.01 ≈ 4.6. One very confident mistake can outweigh many good predictions, which is why log loss is sensitive to calibration. A useful baseline is the log loss of always predicting the base rate.

Example: a click model predicts 0.8, 0.3 and 0.6 for three impressions with labels 1, 0 and 1. The losses are 0.22, 0.36 and 0.51, so log loss ≈ 0.36.
concepts.mixup: Log loss as a metric is the same quantity as binary cross-entropy used as a training loss. It scores probabilities, not labels, so two models with the same accuracy can have very different log loss.

concepts.name: Mean absolute error
concepts.summary: The average size of the errors, ignoring their sign, in the same units as the target.
concepts.body:
MAE = (1/n) Σ |yᵢ − ŷᵢ|. Every unit of error counts the same, so an error of 10 counts exactly twice as much as an error of 5. That makes it fairly robust to a few large outliers and easy to explain: "on average we are off by 6 minutes."

The constant prediction that minimizes MAE is the median, not the mean, and a model trained on MAE learns the conditional median. That matters for skewed targets such as delivery times or order values.

Example: a delivery-time model predicts 30, 45 and 20 minutes and the real times are 35, 40 and 30. The errors are 5, 5 and 10, so MAE = 20 / 3 ≈ 6.7 minutes.
concepts.mixup: MAE and RMSE use the same units but answer different questions. RMSE is always at least as large as MAE, and the gap grows when a few errors are large. Optimizing MAE pulls predictions toward the median, RMSE toward the mean.

concepts.name: Root mean squared error
concepts.summary: The square root of the average squared error. It is in the target's units and penalizes large errors much more than small ones.
concepts.body:
RMSE = √((1/n) Σ (yᵢ − ŷᵢ)²). Mean squared error (MSE) is the same thing without the square root. Squaring means an error of 10 counts four times as much as an error of 5, so RMSE suits problems where big misses are much worse than small ones, such as forecasting warehouse stock.

The prediction that minimizes squared error is the mean, and a model trained on it learns the conditional mean. RMSE is sensitive to outliers and to a few badly predicted rows, so look at the error distribution, not just the single number.

Example: with errors of 5, 5 and 10 minutes, MSE = (25 + 25 + 100) / 3 = 50 and RMSE = √50 ≈ 7.1 minutes. MAE on the same errors is 6.7.
concepts.mixup: RMSE is not the average error. It is always at least MAE, and equal only when every error has the same size. A model with lower MAE can still have higher RMSE if it makes a few big mistakes.

concepts.name: R-squared
concepts.summary: The share of the target's variance that a regression model explains, compared with always predicting the mean.
concepts.body:
R² = 1 − SS_res / SS_tot, where SS_res = Σ (yᵢ − ŷᵢ)² and SS_tot = Σ (yᵢ − ȳ)². A score of 1 is a perfect fit, 0 is no better than predicting the mean, and on held-out data it goes negative when the model does worse than the mean.

R² has no units, which makes it handy for comparing models on the same target. But it says nothing about the size of errors in business terms, and a high R² can hide a model that is badly wrong on an important slice. Report it next to MAE or RMSE.

Example: for a house-price model, SS_tot = 400 and SS_res = 100 on the test set. R² = 1 − 100 / 400 = 0.75.
concepts.mixup: R² is not always the square of a correlation. That only holds for least squares linear regression with an intercept, scored on its own training data. On a test set R² can be below zero. Adding features never lowers training R², which is why adjusted R² exists.

concepts.name: Macro and micro averaging
concepts.summary: Two ways to combine a metric across classes. Macro averages the per-class scores equally. Micro pools all the counts first.
concepts.body:
Macro averaging computes the metric for each class, then takes the plain mean, so a rare class counts as much as a common one. Micro averaging adds up TP, FP and FN across all classes and computes the metric once, so common classes dominate. Weighted averaging takes the mean of per-class scores weighted by each class's support.

For single-label multiclass problems, micro precision, micro recall and micro F1 all equal accuracy.

Example: a ticket classifier has 900 billing tickets with F1 0.95 and 100 legal tickets with F1 0.40. Macro F1 = (0.95 + 0.40) / 2 = 0.675. Weighted F1 = 0.9 × 0.95 + 0.1 × 0.40 = 0.895. Only the macro number shows that the legal class is failing.

Report macro when every class matters, such as rare but serious ticket types.
concepts.mixup: Micro F1 sounds balanced but is not. In single-label multiclass problems it is just accuracy, so it hides a failing rare class. Macro is the average that treats each class equally.

concepts.name: NDCG
concepts.summary: A ranking metric that rewards putting the most relevant items near the top, scaled so a perfect ordering scores 1.
concepts.body:
Discounted cumulative gain adds up the relevance of each result, divided by a log of its position: DCG@k = Σ relᵢ / log₂(i + 1) for positions i = 1 to k. Some systems use 2^rel − 1 as the gain to reward highly relevant items more. NDCG@k divides DCG@k by the DCG of the ideal ordering (IDCG), giving a score from 0 to 1 for each query, then averages across queries.

It handles graded relevance, such as 0 to 3, and cares about order, which makes it a standard metric for search and recommendation.

Example: the top 3 results have relevance 3, 0 and 2. DCG = 3/1 + 0/1.585 + 2/2 = 4.0. The ideal order 3, 2, 0 gives IDCG = 3 + 2/1.585 + 0 ≈ 4.26. NDCG@3 = 4.0 / 4.26 ≈ 0.94.
concepts.mixup: The ideal ordering should be built from all items judged relevant for the query, not only the items the model returned. Using only the returned items inflates NDCG for a model that misses good results entirely.

concepts.name: Precision@k and recall@k
concepts.summary: Precision@k is the share of the top k results that are relevant. Recall@k is the share of all relevant items that appear in the top k.
concepts.body:
For one query, precision@k = (relevant items in top k) / k and recall@k = (relevant items in top k) / (total relevant items). Scores are then averaged across queries or users.

Both ignore the order inside the top k, and neither uses graded relevance. Precision@k suits a fixed number of slots, such as 5 product tiles on a home page. Recall@k suits the first stage of a retrieval or RAG system, where the job is to get the right items into a candidate set that a reranker or LLM will use next.

Example: a user has 4 relevant articles, and the top 10 recommendations contain 3 of them. Precision@10 = 3 / 10 = 0.30 and recall@10 = 3 / 4 = 0.75.
concepts.mixup: Precision@k is capped when a query has fewer than k relevant items. With 2 relevant items, precision@10 can never pass 0.20. Recall@k has no such cap but rises as k grows, so always compare models at the same k.

concepts.name: Mean reciprocal rank
concepts.summary: The average, across queries, of one divided by the position of the first relevant result.
concepts.body:
For each query, find the rank of the first relevant item and take 1 / rank. A hit at position 1 scores 1, position 2 scores 0.5, position 4 scores 0.25, and no hit in the list scores 0. MRR is the mean of these across queries.

It fits tasks where the user needs one good answer: question answering, navigational search, or checking whether a RAG retriever puts a correct passage near the top. It ignores every relevant item after the first.

Example: three queries have their first relevant result at rank 1, at rank 3, and nowhere in the list. MRR = (1 + 1/3 + 0) / 3 ≈ 0.44.
concepts.mixup: MRR only sees the first relevant item, so it cannot tell whether the rest of the list is good. Use NDCG or recall@k when several results matter. Also, MRR is not one divided by the mean rank.

concepts.name: A/B testing
concepts.summary: An online experiment that randomly splits users between the current system and a change, then compares a chosen metric to see whether the change caused a real difference.
concepts.body:
Users or sessions are randomly assigned to control (A) or treatment (B). Randomization means the only systematic difference between the groups is the change, so a gap in the metric can be read as caused by it.

Before starting, fix the primary metric, guardrail metrics such as latency or complaints, the smallest effect worth detecting, and the sample size from a power calculation. Run for the planned duration, ideally whole weeks, then test the difference with a significance test or confidence interval.

Example: a new ranking model goes to 50% of users for two weeks. Click-through rises from 4.0% to 4.2%, with a 95% confidence interval of +0.05 to +0.35 points, so the lift is unlikely to be noise.

Common traps are stopping early when the result looks good, checking many metrics without correction, novelty effects, and groups that affect each other, such as buyers sharing marketplace stock.
concepts.mixup: A p-value below 0.05 does not mean a 95% chance the change works. It means a difference this large would be unlikely if there were no real effect. Statistical significance is also not business significance, so check the size of the effect.

concepts.name: Offline vs online evaluation
concepts.summary: Offline evaluation scores a model on held-out historical data. Online evaluation measures its effect on real users or live traffic.
concepts.body:
Offline evaluation is cheap, fast and repeatable. You compute metrics such as AUC, NDCG or RMSE on a test set before anything ships. Online evaluation uses live traffic through A/B tests, interleaving, shadow or canary deployments, and measures outcomes such as conversion, retention or resolved tickets.

The two often disagree. Historical data was shaped by the old model through feedback loops and position bias, the offline metric may be a weak proxy for the business goal, and live features may differ from training features (training-serving skew).

Example: a new recommender lifts offline NDCG by 4% but loses on click-through in an A/B test, because it keeps recommending items users have already bought. Offline wins decide what is worth testing online, not what ships.
concepts.mixup: A better offline metric does not guarantee a better product. Treat offline evaluation as the gate that decides which candidates earn an online test, and treat the online result as the decision.

concepts.name: Slice-based evaluation
concepts.summary: Measuring a model's metrics separately on meaningful subgroups of the data, so weaknesses hidden by the overall average become visible.
concepts.body:
An overall score averages over everyone, and a model can be good on average while failing badly for one group. Slice-based evaluation splits the test set by things like country, device, new versus returning users, language or product category, and reports the metric for each slice with its sample size.

It is how you find problems before users do, check fairness across groups, and confirm a new model does not regress on an important segment even when its average improves.

Example: a fraud model has recall 0.85 overall. Split by payment method, recall is 0.90 on cards but 0.40 on bank transfers, which are a small share of traffic but a large share of losses.

Small slices give noisy numbers, so show confidence intervals and do not chase every dip.
concepts.mixup: Slice-based evaluation is not stratified sampling. Stratification controls how data is split, so each part keeps the class or group mix. Slicing is how you report results after the split. You often use both together.

concepts.name: BLEU and ROUGE
concepts.summary: Two families of metrics that score generated text by its n-gram overlap with reference texts. BLEU is precision-based and ROUGE is recall-oriented.
concepts.body:
BLEU, built for machine translation, computes clipped n-gram precision for n = 1 to 4, takes their geometric mean, and multiplies by a brevity penalty so very short outputs cannot score well. It is usually reported over a whole corpus.

ROUGE, built for summarization, measures how much of the reference appears in the output. ROUGE-N counts overlapping n-grams and ROUGE-L uses the longest common subsequence. Most tools report ROUGE as an F-measure as well as recall.

Both are cheap and reproducible but reward surface wording. "The meeting was cancelled" and "They called off the meeting" mean the same yet share few n-grams. For open-ended LLM output, teams pair them with human review, semantic similarity or LLM-as-judge.

Example: the output "the cat sat on the mat" against the reference "the cat is on the mat" matches 5 of its 6 words, so unigram precision is 5/6 ≈ 0.83.
concepts.mixup: A higher BLEU or ROUGE does not mean a better answer. Both measure overlap with one or a few references, so a correct paraphrase can score low and a fluent but wrong answer that copies key phrases can score high.

concepts.name: Data leakage
concepts.summary: When information that would not be available at prediction time gets into training or evaluation, so offline results look better than real performance.
concepts.body:
Leakage makes a model look great offline and disappoint in production. It comes in a few common forms:

- Target leakage: a feature is caused by, or recorded after, the label.
- Train-test contamination: the same or near-duplicate rows, users or documents appear in both training and test data.
- Preprocessing leakage: scalers, imputers or feature selection fitted on the full dataset before splitting.
- Temporal leakage: using the future to predict the past, such as a random split on time-ordered data.

Example: a churn model scores AUC 0.99 offline. Its top feature is "account closure reason", which is only filled in after the customer leaves. In production that field is always empty.

A suspiciously high score, or one feature that dominates the importance chart, is the classic warning sign.
concepts.mixup: Leakage is not overfitting. An overfit model does badly on the held-out set. A leaky model does well on the held-out set, because the held-out set is contaminated too, and only fails once it meets real production data.

concepts.name: Target leakage
concepts.summary: Leakage where a feature carries information about the label that would not exist at the moment the prediction is made.
concepts.body:
The feature is usually a consequence of the outcome or is recorded after it, so the model learns to read the answer instead of predicting it.

Ask of every feature: at the exact moment this prediction is made in production, would this value be known, and would it have this value? If not, drop it or rebuild it as of that moment.

Examples:
- Predicting pneumonia with a feature "took antibiotics", which is usually recorded because the patient was already diagnosed.
- Predicting loan default with "number of collection calls".
- Predicting whether a support ticket escalates using "time to resolution", which is only known once the ticket closes.

Warning signs are near-perfect validation scores and a single feature with huge importance. Check that feature's timestamp against the prediction time.
concepts.mixup: Target leakage is not the same as a strong feature. A feature can be highly predictive and perfectly legitimate. The test is timing: was the value known before the outcome, at the moment the model would really be called?

concepts.name: Preprocessing leakage
concepts.summary: Leakage caused by fitting a preprocessing step, such as a scaler, imputer or feature selector, on data that includes the validation or test rows.
concepts.body:
Any step that learns from data has parameters. A scaler learns means and standard deviations, an imputer learns fill values, a feature selector learns which columns track the label, and a target encoder learns category means. If those are fitted before the split, statistics from the test rows shape the training data and the test score is optimistic.

The fix is to split first, fit every step on the training fold only, and apply it unchanged to the other rows. In scikit-learn, put the steps in a `Pipeline` and pass the pipeline to `cross_val_score` or `GridSearchCV`, so each fold refits them.

Example: from 10,000 pure-noise features, pick the 20 most correlated with the label using all rows, then cross-validate. Accuracy looks far above chance. Done inside each fold, it drops back to chance.
concepts.mixup: Scaling with the full-data mean and standard deviation is usually a small leak. Supervised steps, such as feature selection or target encoding fitted on all rows, can be a huge one. Both are wrong, but the second is the one that fakes a good model.

concepts.name: Point-in-time correctness
concepts.summary: Building each training example only from feature values as they were known at that example's prediction time, never from later values.
concepts.body:
Features change over time. A customer's lifetime spend, account status or risk score today is not what it was six months ago. If a training row for a January prediction pulls today's value, the model trains on information from the future.

A point-in-time join, also called an as-of join, fixes this. For each label event at time t, it takes the latest feature value with a timestamp at or before t. Feature stores do this when they build training sets, and pandas `merge_asof` applies the same idea.

Example: to predict on 1 March whether a user will cancel, "support tickets in the last 30 days" must count only tickets opened before 1 March, even though the warehouse now holds tickets from later weeks.

Watch for late-arriving data too. If a value was recorded after t, even with an earlier event time, it was not available at t.
concepts.mixup: Splitting by time is not enough. A time-based split keeps future rows out of training, but each row's features can still be computed with future data. Point-in-time correctness is about how every feature value is built.

concepts.name: Deduplication
concepts.summary: Finding and removing exact or near-duplicate records, so the same example does not appear in both training and test data or skew the training mix.
concepts.body:
Duplicates come from repeated logging, pages copied across websites, merged data sources and augmentation. They cause two problems. Across splits they leak: the model is tested on rows it has already seen, so the score is inflated. Within training they overweight some examples, and in LLM pretraining heavy duplication encourages memorization.

Exact duplicates are found by hashing a normalized record. Near duplicates need fuzzy methods, such as MinHash with locality-sensitive hashing on text shingles, or embedding similarity above a threshold.

Group-aware splitting helps too. If one patient has 10 scans, keep all of them in the same split, for example with `GroupKFold`.

Example: a ticket classifier scores 0.95, but 15% of the test tickets are copy-pasted templates that also appear in training. After deduplication the score falls to 0.88.
concepts.mixup: Removing exact duplicates is not enough. Rows that differ only by a timestamp, whitespace or ID can still leak, and so can different rows from the same user or document. Deduplicate fuzzily and split by group where it matters.

concepts.name: Class imbalance
concepts.summary: When one class is far rarer than the others, so accuracy misleads and models tend to ignore the rare class.
concepts.body:
Fraud, churn, disease and defect detection often have positive rates of 1% or less. A model can score 99% accuracy by always predicting the majority class.

Fix the evaluation first. Use precision, recall, F1, the precision-recall curve or a cost-based metric, and use stratified splits so every fold contains positives. Then tune the decision threshold for the real costs, which is often the most effective single change.

Training-side options include class weights, oversampling the rare class, undersampling the common class, or collecting more positive examples. Strong models such as gradient boosting often rank well without any rebalancing, so a plain model with a tuned threshold is a good baseline.

Example: with 500 frauds in 100,000 transactions, a model that flags nothing has accuracy 0.995 and recall 0.
concepts.mixup: Rebalancing the training data does not fix the evaluation. Always measure on data with the real class ratio. Resampling and class weights also shift predicted probabilities, so recalibrate if you need real probabilities.

concepts.name: Oversampling and undersampling
concepts.summary: Changing the class mix of the training data, by repeating or synthesizing rare examples or by dropping common ones, to help a model learn the rare class.
concepts.body:
Random oversampling duplicates minority rows. SMOTE creates synthetic minority rows by interpolating between a minority example and one of its nearest minority neighbours. Random undersampling drops majority rows, which also speeds up training but throws data away.

Rules that matter:
- Resample only the training data, inside each cross-validation fold, never before splitting. Otherwise copies of one row land in both train and validation.
- Evaluate on data with the real class ratio.
- Resampling shifts predicted probabilities toward the rare class. Recalibrate, or correct for the sampling rate, if you need real probabilities.

Example: with 1,000 frauds and 99,000 normal rows, undersampling the normal rows to 9,000 gives a 10% fraud rate for training. A model trained on that will overestimate fraud probability on live traffic unless corrected.
concepts.mixup: SMOTE is not a free gain. On many tabular problems a tuned model with class weights or a tuned threshold does as well or better, and SMOTE can create unrealistic rows. Oversampling before the train-test split is a classic leakage bug.

concepts.name: Class weights
concepts.summary: Giving errors on some classes, usually the rare class, a bigger weight in the loss, so the model pays more attention to them without changing the data.
concepts.body:
Each training example's loss is multiplied by the weight of its class. A weight of 10 on fraud makes one missed fraud cost as much as ten mistakes on normal transactions during training. The effect is similar to oversampling, without duplicating rows.

In scikit-learn, `class_weight="balanced"` sets each weight to n_samples / (n_classes × n_samples_in_class). With 95,000 negatives and 5,000 positives, the weights are about 0.53 and 10. In PyTorch, `CrossEntropyLoss` takes a `weight` argument and `BCEWithLogitsLoss` takes `pos_weight`.

Weights change what the model optimizes, so its predicted probabilities no longer match real rates. If you need calibrated probabilities, recalibrate on unweighted validation data, or keep weights at 1 and tune the threshold instead.
concepts.mixup: Class weights and the decision threshold are often confused. Weights change how the model trains. The threshold changes how scores become labels after training. For a model that already ranks well, tuning the threshold alone often gives a similar result.

concepts.name: Imputation
concepts.summary: Filling in missing values with estimates so a model can use rows that have gaps.
concepts.body:
Simple methods fill each column with its mean, median or most common value, or with a constant such as 0 or "unknown". Model-based methods predict the missing value from other columns, such as k-nearest neighbours or iterative imputation in the style of MICE. For time series, forward fill carries the last known value forward.

Two habits matter. Fit the imputer on training data only, so test-set statistics do not leak. And add a missing-indicator column, because the fact that a value is missing is often predictive itself, such as a blank income field on a loan application.

Some models handle missing values natively. Gradient-boosted trees such as XGBoost, LightGBM and scikit-learn's HistGradientBoosting learn which branch missing values should follow.

Example: ages 25, 40, missing and 31. Median imputation fills the gap with 31, the median of the three known values.
concepts.mixup: Mean imputation is not neutral. It shrinks the column's variance and weakens its correlations with other columns. The right method depends on why the data is missing, so check the missing data mechanism first.

concepts.name: Missing data mechanisms
concepts.summary: The three reasons data can be missing: completely at random, at random given other observed data, or depending on the missing value itself.
concepts.body:
- **MCAR** (missing completely at random): missingness has nothing to do with any data. A sensor drops readings because of random network loss. Dropping those rows loses data but does not bias results.
- **MAR** (missing at random): missingness depends only on observed columns. Older customers skip the email field more often, and age is recorded. Imputation that uses age can correct for it.
- **MNAR** (missing not at random): missingness depends on the unobserved value itself. People with very high incomes leave income blank. No method using only the observed data can fully fix this, so you need domain knowledge, a missing indicator, or better data collection.

You can find evidence against MCAR by checking whether missingness correlates with other columns. MNAR cannot be confirmed from the observed data alone.
concepts.mixup: Missing at random does not mean random in the everyday sense. MAR allows missingness to depend on other observed columns. Only MCAR means the gaps are unrelated to everything.

concepts.name: Feature scaling
concepts.summary: Putting numeric features on comparable ranges, so models that depend on distances or gradient steps are not dominated by features with large units.
concepts.body:
Standardization subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation: z = (x − μ) / σ. Min-max scaling maps values to [0, 1] with (x − min) / (max − min). Robust scaling uses the median and interquartile range, so outliers matter less. A log transform helps heavily skewed features such as income.

Scaling matters for k-nearest neighbours, k-means, SVMs, PCA, and linear or neural models trained with gradient descent or regularization. Tree models split on thresholds, so scaling does not change them.

Fit the scaler on training data only, then apply the same parameters to validation, test and production data.

Example: in k-NN on raw values, a 1,000 difference in income outweighs a 40-year difference in age. After standardizing, both are measured in standard deviations and count fairly.
concepts.mixup: Normalization means different things to different people: min-max scaling, z-scoring, or scaling each row to unit length as scikit-learn's `Normalizer` does. Say which one you mean. Scaling also does not remove skew or outliers.

concepts.name: One-hot encoding
concepts.summary: Turning a categorical feature into one binary column per category, with a 1 in the column that matches each row's value.
concepts.body:
A colour column with values red, green and blue becomes three columns: is_red, is_green and is_blue. Exactly one is 1 in each row. Unlike mapping categories to 0, 1 and 2, this does not invent an order or distance between them.

Practical points:
- High cardinality explodes the width. A city column with 20,000 values becomes 20,000 sparse columns. Group rare categories into "other", or use target encoding, feature hashing or embeddings.
- Categories that appear in production but not in training must be handled, for example with `handle_unknown="ignore"` in scikit-learn, which encodes them as all zeros.
- With a linear model that has an intercept, the full set of columns is perfectly collinear, the dummy variable trap. Drop one column or use regularization.

Fit the category list on training data only.
concepts.mixup: One-hot encoding is not label encoding. Label encoding gives each category an integer, which tree models can often cope with, but it tells linear and distance-based models that category 3 sits between categories 2 and 4.

concepts.name: Target encoding
concepts.summary: Replacing each category with a statistic of the target for that category, usually the mean label, often smoothed toward the overall mean.
concepts.body:
For a binary target, each category becomes the share of positives among its training rows. That turns a high-cardinality column, such as merchant ID or postcode, into a single dense number.

Because the encoding is built from the label, it leaks easily. A row's own label feeds into its encoded value, so rare categories look perfectly predictive in training. Two standard fixes:
- Compute it out of fold: each training row gets statistics from the other folds only. scikit-learn's `TargetEncoder` does this in `fit_transform`.
- Smooth toward the global mean: encoded = (n × category mean + m × global mean) / (n + m), where n is the category count and m sets how strongly to shrink.

Example: a merchant has 3 transactions and 2 are fraud, a raw mean of 0.67. With a global fraud rate of 0.01 and m = 10, the smoothed value is (2 + 0.1) / 13 ≈ 0.16.
concepts.mixup: Target encoding fitted on all training rows and then used to train on those same rows is target leakage, because each encoded value is partly made from the label being predicted. Cross-fitting and smoothing are not optional extras.

concepts.name: Feature hashing
concepts.summary: Mapping features or categories into a fixed number of columns with a hash function, so you never need to store a vocabulary.
concepts.body:
Each category, or each token in text, is hashed, and the hash modulo n picks one of n columns. A second hash often sets the sign to +1 or −1, so collisions tend to cancel rather than pile up.

Memory stays fixed no matter how many categories appear, new categories in production need no refitting, and there is no fitting step at all. It is common in ad click and text models with millions of sparse features.

The cost is collisions: unrelated categories share a column, which adds noise, and columns cannot be mapped back to names, which hurts interpretability. More columns mean fewer collisions.

Example: hashing 1 million distinct user-agent strings into 2²⁰ ≈ 1.05 million columns still leaves about 60% of the strings sharing a column with at least one other. Collisions start long before the columns fill up.
concepts.mixup: Feature hashing is not an embedding. Hashing is a fixed, random mapping with no learned meaning. Embeddings are learned vectors where similar items end up close. Hashed IDs are often fed into a learned embedding table, which combines the two.

concepts.name: Feature selection
concepts.summary: Choosing a subset of the available features to keep, to cut noise, cost and overfitting while keeping predictive power.
concepts.body:
There are three families:
- **Filter methods** score each feature on its own, with correlation, mutual information or a chi-squared test, and keep the top ones. Fast, but blind to interactions.
- **Wrapper methods** train models on different subsets and keep the best, such as recursive feature elimination (RFE). More accurate but expensive.
- **Embedded methods** select during training, such as L1 regularization pushing weights to zero, or tree-based importance.

Selection must happen inside the cross-validation loop, fitted only on training folds. Selecting on all the data first and then cross-validating leaks the label and can make pure noise look predictive.

In production, fewer features also mean fewer pipelines to maintain and fewer inputs that can break or drift.

Example: a churn model with 300 features keeps the same validation AUC with the top 40, and the team stops maintaining 260 upstream feeds.
concepts.mixup: Low importance in one model does not mean a feature is useless. Correlated features share importance, so dropping one of a pair may barely matter while dropping both hurts. Check performance after removal, not just importance scores.

concepts.name: Outliers
concepts.summary: Data points far from the rest of the distribution. Some are errors to fix or remove, and some are real cases the model must learn.
concepts.body:
Common rules flag values more than 3 standard deviations from the mean (z-score), or more than 1.5 × IQR below the first quartile or above the third (Tukey's fences). For many features at once, use isolation forest or a distance-based method.

The key question is why the point is extreme. A human height of 2,500 cm is a data entry error to fix or remove. A $50,000 purchase on a card that usually spends $50 might be exactly the fraud you want to catch.

For real but extreme values you can cap them (winsorize), apply a log transform, use robust scaling, or use a loss that is less sensitive, such as MAE or Huber loss instead of squared error. Tree models are fairly robust to outliers in features, but not to outliers in a target fitted with squared error.

Example: with Q1 = 20 and Q3 = 40, the IQR is 20, so Tukey's rule flags values below −10 or above 70.
concepts.mixup: Removing outliers is not always cleaning. In fraud, safety and anomaly detection, the outliers are often the signal. Remove only points you can show are errors, and never drop test rows to make a metric look better.

concepts.name: Label noise
concepts.summary: Wrong labels in the training or evaluation data, caused by annotator mistakes, unclear guidelines or automated labeling rules.
concepts.body:
Noise can be random, such as a tired annotator's slip, or systematic, such as a guideline that makes everyone label sarcasm as positive. Systematic noise is worse, because the model learns the bias faithfully.

Noise in training data caps how well a model can learn and encourages large models to memorize wrong examples. Noise in the test set is sneakier: it caps the measurable score and can make the better model look worse.

To find and reduce it, measure inter-annotator agreement, clarify guidelines, have several annotators label hard items, and review examples where a cross-validated model confidently disagrees with the label, which is the idea behind confident learning. Robust losses and label smoothing limit the damage during training.

Example: if 5% of a spam classifier's test labels are wrong, even a perfect model scores only about 0.95 accuracy, and a 1-point gap between models may be noise.
concepts.mixup: More data does not wash out systematic label noise. Random noise averages out with enough examples, but a consistent bias in how items were labeled is learned as if it were the truth.

concepts.name: Inter-annotator agreement
concepts.summary: How consistently different people label the same items, usually reported with a chance-corrected score such as Cohen's kappa.
concepts.body:
Raw percent agreement misleads when one label is common, because two annotators who mostly say "not spam" agree often by chance. Cohen's kappa corrects for this with two annotators: κ = (pₒ − pₑ) / (1 − pₑ), where pₒ is observed agreement and pₑ is the agreement expected by chance from each annotator's label rates. Fleiss' kappa and Krippendorff's alpha handle more annotators.

Low agreement usually means vague guidelines or a truly ambiguous task, not lazy annotators. It also limits evaluation: when humans agree only 80% of the time, a model's score against one person's labels is hard to interpret above that level.

Example: two annotators agree on 90% of support tickets, and each labels 80% as routine. Chance agreement is 0.8 × 0.8 + 0.2 × 0.2 = 0.68, so κ = (0.90 − 0.68) / 0.32 ≈ 0.69.
concepts.mixup: High percent agreement does not mean reliable labels. With a dominant class, 90% agreement can give a modest kappa, and a kappa near 0 means agreement no better than chance even when raw agreement looks high.

concepts.name: Active learning
concepts.summary: A labeling strategy where the model picks which unlabeled examples a human should label next, to get more accuracy per label.
concepts.body:
The loop is: train on the labeled set, score the unlabeled pool, send the most useful examples to annotators, add the new labels, and retrain. Common ways to pick examples:
- **Uncertainty sampling**: items the model is least sure about, such as probabilities near 0.5 or high entropy.
- **Query by committee**: items where several models disagree most.
- **Diversity sampling**: items from different parts of the data, so a batch is not 100 near-copies of one confusing case.

It pays off when labels are expensive, such as medical images or legal documents, and unlabeled data is plentiful.

Example: a moderation team can afford 2,000 labels. Instead of a random 2,000 posts, mostly obvious cases, each round they label the posts the current model is least sure about.

The labeled set is no longer a random sample, so keep a separate randomly drawn test set for honest evaluation.
concepts.mixup: Active learning is not semi-supervised learning. Active learning asks humans for new labels on chosen examples. Semi-supervised learning uses unlabeled data directly, for example through pseudo-labels, without asking for more human labels.

concepts.name: Stratified sampling
concepts.summary: Sampling or splitting data so each subgroup, usually each class, keeps the same proportion in every part as in the whole.
concepts.body:
With a rare class, a random split can leave a validation fold with few or no positives, which makes metrics noisy or undefined. A stratified split keeps the class ratio the same in each part. In scikit-learn, pass `stratify=y` to `train_test_split` or use `StratifiedKFold`.

You can also stratify on other variables, such as region or device, when every part needs to represent them. In surveys and labeling, stratified sampling draws a set number from each group, so small but important groups get enough examples.

Example: 1,000 claims include 20 frauds, split 80/20. A stratified split puts exactly 4 frauds in the test set. A random split could put 1 or 8 there.

Stratification does not replace time-based or group-based splits. If the data is time-ordered or has repeat users, deal with that first.
concepts.mixup: Stratified sampling is not resampling to balance classes. Stratification keeps the original class ratio in each split. Oversampling and undersampling change the ratio on purpose, and only in the training data.

concepts.name: Selection bias
concepts.summary: When the data you train or evaluate on does not represent the population the model will serve, because of how examples were chosen.
concepts.body:
It enters through how data was collected, not through errors in single rows. Common forms:
- **Sampling bias**: data comes from one channel, region or user type, such as training a loan model only on online applicants.
- **Survivorship bias**: only cases that survived are recorded, such as studying only customers who stayed a full year.
- **Selective labels**: you only see outcomes for cases the old system acted on. A credit model learns repayment only for approved applicants, never for rejected ones.

Selection bias also drives feedback loops: a recommender trained on clicks from its own recommendations only learns about items it chose to show.

Fixes include collecting data more broadly, keeping a small randomized slice of traffic, reweighting by inverse propensity, and comparing your data against the target population slice by slice.
concepts.mixup: More data from the same source does not fix selection bias. A million biased examples are still biased. It also differs from label noise: every label can be correct and the sample still unrepresentative.

concepts.name: Data validation
concepts.summary: Automatic checks that data matches what the model expects, run before training and before serving, so bad data is caught before it reaches a model.
concepts.body:
Typical checks:
- **Schema**: expected columns exist with the right types.
- **Ranges and values**: ages between 0 and 120, categories from a known set, no negative prices.
- **Completeness**: null rates within limits and row counts close to normal.
- **Uniqueness**: no duplicate keys.
- **Distribution**: feature distributions close to a reference, measured with PSI or a statistical test.

Validation is cheap insurance. Many production ML failures start as data problems: an upstream team renames a field, a unit changes from dollars to cents, or a pipeline silently writes nulls. Without checks, the model keeps serving confident predictions on broken inputs.

Example: a nightly job checks that the null rate of device_type stays under 2%. After an app release it jumps to 60%, and the check blocks the retraining run instead of training a model on broken data.
concepts.mixup: Data validation is not the same as model monitoring. Validation checks inputs against rules and a reference before they are used. Monitoring watches predictions and outcomes over time after deployment. You need both.

concepts.name: Multilayer perceptron
concepts.summary: A neural network made of stacked fully connected layers, each a linear map followed by a nonlinear activation.
concepts.body:
An MLP passes the input through a stack of layers. Each layer computes h = f(Wx + b), where W is a weight matrix, b a bias vector and f a nonlinear activation such as ReLU. The output layer has no activation for regression, or a sigmoid or softmax for classification.

The nonlinearity is what gives the network its power. With one wide enough hidden layer, an MLP can approximate any continuous function on a bounded input range (the universal approximation theorem), although that says nothing about how easy it is to train. MLPs are a common model for tabular inputs in deep pipelines, and one sits inside every transformer block as the feed-forward sublayer.

Example: a churn model takes 20 features, has hidden layers of 64 and 32 units and one output unit. It has (20×64 + 64) + (64×32 + 32) + (32×1 + 1) = 1,344 + 2,080 + 33 = 3,457 parameters.
concepts.mixup: Stacking linear layers without activations does not make a deep network. The product of the weight matrices is still one linear map, so the model can only learn what a single linear layer can.

concepts.name: Activation function
concepts.summary: A nonlinear function applied to each neuron's output so that stacked layers can learn curved, non-linear patterns.
concepts.body:
After a layer computes z = Wx + b, an activation f is applied to each element. Common choices:

- ReLU: max(0, z). Cheap, and keeps gradients alive for positive inputs. A default in many CNNs and MLPs.
- GELU and SiLU (also called Swish): smooth versions of ReLU, common in transformers.
- Sigmoid: 1 / (1 + e⁻ᶻ), squashes to (0, 1). Used for binary outputs and gates.
- Tanh: squashes to (−1, 1) and is zero-centred. Used in RNN cells.

The choice affects how gradients flow. Sigmoid and tanh saturate for large |z|, where their slope is near zero, which feeds vanishing gradients in deep stacks. A ReLU unit can get stuck outputting zero for every input, called a dying ReLU. Leaky ReLU, with a small slope such as 0.01 for z < 0, avoids that.

Example: for z = [−2, 0.5, 3], ReLU gives [0, 0.5, 3].
concepts.mixup: Softmax is often listed with activations, but it does not act on each element alone. It normalizes a whole vector into probabilities and belongs on the output layer, not inside hidden layers.

concepts.name: Softmax
concepts.summary: Turns a vector of raw scores, called logits, into probabilities that are all positive and sum to 1.
concepts.body:
softmax(zᵢ) = e^(zᵢ) / Σⱼ e^(zⱼ). Exponentiating makes every value positive, and dividing by the sum makes them add to 1. Larger logits get a disproportionately larger share.

It is the output layer of almost every multi-class classifier and of every language model, where it turns scores over the vocabulary into a next-token distribution. It also sits inside attention, turning similarity scores into weights.

In code you subtract the largest logit first. softmax(z) = softmax(z − max z), so the result is unchanged, but e^z can no longer overflow.

Example: logits [2, 1, 0] give e² ≈ 7.39, e¹ ≈ 2.72 and e⁰ = 1. The sum is about 11.11, so the probabilities are about [0.67, 0.24, 0.09].
concepts.mixup: Softmax is for picking one label out of many, where classes compete for probability. For multi-label problems, where an item can carry several labels at once, use an independent sigmoid on each output instead.

concepts.name: Cross-entropy loss
concepts.summary: The standard classification loss: the negative log of the probability the model gave to the correct class.
concepts.body:
For one example with true class y and predicted probabilities p, the loss is −log p_y. With one-hot or soft targets t it is −Σ tᵢ log pᵢ. The binary case is −[y log p + (1 − y) log(1 − p)]. Averaged over a dataset, it is the negative log-likelihood of the labels.

It punishes confident mistakes hard. Giving the true class 0.9 costs −ln 0.9 ≈ 0.105. Giving it 0.01 costs −ln 0.01 ≈ 4.6. Paired with softmax, its gradient with respect to the logits is simply p − t, which stays large when the model is badly wrong. That is why it trains much better than squared error on probabilities.

Many framework loss functions take raw logits and apply log-softmax inside for numerical stability, so check the docs before applying softmax yourself. Language models use the same loss on every next token.
concepts.mixup: Loss and accuracy can disagree. Cross-entropy can keep falling while accuracy stays flat, because the model grows more confident on examples it already gets right. Validation loss can also rise while accuracy holds, a sign of overconfident mistakes.

concepts.name: Backpropagation
concepts.summary: The algorithm that computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight by applying the chain rule backwards through the network.
concepts.body:
Training has two passes. The forward pass computes each layer's output and the loss, storing intermediate activations. The backward pass starts from ∂L/∂output and moves layer by layer toward the input. At each layer it uses the chain rule to get the gradient for that layer's weights and the gradient to pass further back. An optimizer such as SGD or Adam then uses those gradients to update the weights.

As a rule of thumb, the backward pass costs about twice the forward pass, and the stored activations are a main driver of training memory. That is why gradient checkpointing trades extra recomputation for lower memory.

Example: for y = w·x with loss L = (y − t)², the gradient is ∂L/∂w = 2(y − t)·x. With w = 2, x = 3 and t = 5, the prediction is y = 6 and the gradient is 2 × 1 × 3 = 6.
concepts.mixup: Backpropagation only computes gradients. Gradient descent, or another optimizer, is the separate step that uses them to change the weights. Saying backprop updates the weights blurs the two.

concepts.name: Vanishing gradients
concepts.summary: Gradients shrink toward zero as they are passed back through many layers, so the early layers barely learn.
concepts.body:
Backpropagation multiplies one local derivative per layer. If those factors are mostly below 1, the product shrinks exponentially with depth. If they are mostly above 1, it blows up instead, which is the exploding-gradient problem.

The sigmoid's slope is at most 0.25, so ten sigmoid layers can scale a gradient by 0.25¹⁰ ≈ 10⁻⁶. The first layers then get almost no signal and the loss stalls. Plain RNNs suffer the same thing across time steps, which is why they struggle with long-range dependencies.

The fixes that made deep networks trainable are ReLU-family activations, careful initialization (Xavier or He), normalization layers, residual connections that give gradients a direct path, and gated cells such as LSTM and GRU for sequences. Exploding gradients are usually handled with gradient clipping.

A sign in practice: gradient norms in the first layers are orders of magnitude smaller than in the last ones.
concepts.mixup: A flat training loss is not proof of vanishing gradients. A learning rate that is too low, or a broken data pipeline, looks the same. Check per-layer gradient norms before changing the architecture.

concepts.name: Gradient clipping
concepts.summary: Capping the size of the gradient before each update so one bad batch cannot throw the weights far off course.
concepts.body:
The common form is clipping by global norm. Compute the L2 norm g of all gradients together. If g is above a threshold c, scale every gradient by c / g. The direction stays the same and only the step length shrinks. Clipping by value instead caps each element at ±c, which can change the direction.

It guards against exploding gradients, which show up as sudden loss spikes or NaNs. It is standard when training RNNs and transformers, and as a rule of thumb a threshold of 1.0 is a common starting point.

Example: the global gradient norm is 8 and the threshold is 1. Every gradient is multiplied by 1 / 8 = 0.125, so the total norm becomes 1.

Logging the norm before clipping is a cheap health check. If clipping fires on almost every step, the learning rate or the data probably needs a look.
concepts.mixup: Clipping limits how big a step can be. It does nothing for vanishing gradients, which are too small rather than too large. Residual connections, normalization and good initialization address that problem.

concepts.name: Weight initialization
concepts.summary: Choosing the starting values of a network's weights so signals and gradients keep a stable size through every layer.
concepts.body:
If all weights start equal, every neuron in a layer computes the same thing and gets the same gradient, so they never become different. Random values break this symmetry. Their scale then decides whether activations shrink, stay steady or explode as they pass through the layers.

The standard rules set the variance from the layer's fan-in (number of inputs) and fan-out (number of outputs):

- Xavier (Glorot): Var(w) = 2 / (fan_in + fan_out), suited to tanh and sigmoid.
- He (Kaiming): Var(w) = 2 / fan_in, suited to ReLU, which zeroes about half its inputs.

Example: a ReLU layer with 512 inputs under He initialization draws weights with standard deviation √(2/512) = 0.0625.

Biases usually start at zero. Frameworks apply sensible defaults, but custom layers and very deep stacks often need deliberate choices, such as scaling down the last layer of each residual branch.
concepts.mixup: Zero is a fine start for biases but not for weights. With all weights at zero, every neuron in a layer stays identical through training. Weights need small random values, with a scale matched to the layer size.

concepts.name: Batch normalization
concepts.summary: A layer that normalizes each feature using the mean and variance of the current mini-batch, then applies a learned scale and shift.
concepts.body:
For each feature, or each channel in a CNN, batch norm computes the batch mean μ and variance σ² and outputs y = γ(x − μ) / √(σ² + ε) + β, where γ and β are learned. This keeps activations in a steady range, which allows higher learning rates and makes training less sensitive to initialization.

The catch is that training and inference behave differently. In training it uses batch statistics and also keeps running averages of μ and σ². At inference it uses those fixed averages, so a prediction does not depend on what else is in the batch. Forgetting to switch the model to evaluation mode is a classic bug.

It works poorly with very small batches, where the statistics are noisy, and is awkward for variable-length sequences. That is why transformers use layer normalization instead.

Example: a CNN layer with 64 channels has 64 values of γ and 64 of β.
concepts.mixup: Batch norm normalizes each feature across the examples in a batch. Layer norm normalizes across the features of a single example. Only batch norm depends on batch size and needs separate training and inference behaviour.

concepts.name: Layer normalization
concepts.summary: Normalizes the features of each example on its own, using that example's mean and variance, then applies a learned scale and shift.
concepts.body:
For one token or example with d features, layer norm computes the mean μ and variance σ² across those d values and outputs y = γ(x − μ) / √(σ² + ε) + β. No other example in the batch is involved.

So it behaves the same in training and inference, works at any batch size including 1, and handles variable-length sequences. Transformers use it around every attention and feed-forward sublayer. Most modern LLMs put it before each sublayer (pre-norm) rather than after the residual add (post-norm), which trains more stably in deep stacks. Many also use RMSNorm, a cheaper variant that skips the mean subtraction and divides by the root mean square.

Example: a token vector [2, 4, 6] has mean 4 and variance 8/3, so before γ and β it becomes about [−1.22, 0, 1.22].
concepts.mixup: The name suggests it normalizes across a whole layer's outputs for the batch. It actually normalizes across the feature dimension of each example separately, which is why batch size does not affect it.

concepts.name: Dropout
concepts.summary: A regularizer that randomly zeroes a fraction of activations during training so the network cannot rely on any single unit.
concepts.body:
With dropout rate p, each activation is set to zero with probability p on every training step. In the usual inverted dropout, the kept activations are divided by (1 − p) so the expected value stays the same. At inference dropout is switched off and every unit is used, with no rescaling needed.

Because a different random subnetwork trains on each step, units cannot co-adapt, which reduces overfitting. It acts like cheaply averaging many thinned networks. As a rule of thumb, rates of 0.1 to 0.5 are typical. Large pretrained LLMs often use little or no dropout, since they see so much data that overfitting is less of a concern.

Example: with p = 0.2, an activation of 1.0 becomes either 0 or 1.0 / 0.8 = 1.25 during training, and stays 1.0 at inference.

Forgetting to switch to evaluation mode leaves dropout on, which makes predictions noisy and different on every call.
concepts.mixup: The dropout rate is the probability of dropping a unit, not of keeping it. Some older code and papers used a keep probability instead, so a value of 0.8 can mean opposite things.

concepts.name: Residual connection
concepts.summary: A shortcut that adds a block's input to its output, y = x + F(x), so the block only has to learn a correction.
concepts.body:
Instead of learning a full mapping, a residual block learns F(x), the change to apply, and outputs x + F(x). If the best move is to do nothing, the block only has to push F toward zero, which is easy.

The bigger benefit is gradient flow. The derivative of x + F(x) with respect to x is 1 + ∂F/∂x, so there is always a direct path for gradients back to early layers. This is what let image networks go from around 20 layers to well over 100, and every transformer block wraps both attention and the feed-forward sublayer in one.

The addition needs matching shapes. When a block changes the channel count or resolution, the shortcut uses a 1×1 convolution or a linear projection to match.

Example: in a pre-norm transformer, the hidden state after the attention sublayer is h + Attention(LayerNorm(h)).
concepts.mixup: Residual connections add the input to the output. DenseNet-style connections and U-Net skips concatenate features instead, which grows the channel count. Both get called skip connections, but they behave differently.

concepts.name: Convolutional neural network
concepts.summary: A network that slides small learned filters over grid data such as images, sharing weights across positions to detect local patterns.
concepts.body:
A convolution layer holds a set of small filters, say 3×3. Each filter slides across the input and computes a weighted sum at every position, producing a feature map. Because the same filter is reused everywhere, the layer has few parameters and spots a pattern wherever it appears. Stacking layers grows the receptive field, so early layers find edges and later ones find parts and objects. Pooling or strides shrink the spatial size along the way.

Output size per side is (n + 2p − k) / s + 1, with the division rounded down, for input size n, padding p, kernel size k and stride s.

Example: a 32×32 RGB image through a 3×3 convolution with 64 filters, padding 1 and stride 1 gives a 32×32×64 output. Parameters: 3×3×3×64 + 64 = 1,792.

CNNs remain strong for images, audio spectrograms and some time series, especially when data or compute is limited.
concepts.mixup: Weight sharing gives translation equivariance, meaning a shifted input gives a shifted feature map. It does not by itself make the network translation invariant. Invariance comes only partly, from pooling and the final global aggregation.

concepts.name: Recurrent neural network
concepts.summary: A network that reads a sequence one step at a time, carrying a hidden state that summarizes everything seen so far.
concepts.body:
At each step t a plain RNN computes hₜ = tanh(W·hₜ₋₁ + U·xₜ + b), using the same weights at every step. The hidden state hₜ is the network's memory and can be used to predict a label or the next item.

Training backpropagates through time across all steps, so gradients are multiplied by the same matrix again and again. They tend to vanish or explode, which makes long-range dependencies hard to learn. LSTM and GRU cells add gates that decide what to keep, forget and output, which keeps gradients alive over much longer spans.

The big limit is that steps must run in order, which blocks parallel training across the sequence. Transformers replaced RNNs for most language tasks largely for this reason. Recurrent designs still appear in streaming and on-device settings, where a fixed-size state per step is attractive.

Example: a 100-word review is read in 100 sequential steps.
concepts.mixup: An LSTM is a type of RNN, not an alternative to one. Its gates ease vanishing gradients but do not remove the step-by-step bottleneck, so it still trains slower than attention on long sequences.

concepts.name: Learning rate
concepts.summary: The number that scales each gradient step, and usually the most important hyperparameter to tune.
concepts.body:
Gradient descent updates weights as w ← w − η·∇L, where η is the learning rate. Too small and training crawls or stalls. Too large and the loss bounces around, spikes or becomes NaN.

The right value depends on the optimizer, the batch size and the model. As rough rules of thumb, Adam-style optimizers often use values around 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻³ when training from scratch and smaller ones for fine-tuning, while SGD with momentum often uses larger values such as 0.1. Rather than guess, run a short sweep on a log scale (10⁻⁵, 3×10⁻⁵, 10⁻⁴ and so on) and pair the chosen peak with a schedule.

Example: with a weight of 0.5, a gradient of 2 and η = 0.1, the new weight is 0.5 − 0.1 × 2 = 0.3.
concepts.mixup: The same learning rate means different things for different optimizers. With plain SGD the step is η times the gradient. With Adam each parameter's step is roughly bounded by η, whatever the gradient's scale, so values do not transfer between the two.

concepts.name: Adam optimizer
concepts.summary: An optimizer that combines momentum with a per-parameter step size scaled by a running estimate of each gradient's squared size.
concepts.body:
Adam keeps two running averages per parameter: m, an average of the gradient g (momentum), and v, an average of g². At step t:

- m ← β₁m + (1 − β₁)g
- v ← β₂v + (1 − β₂)g²
- w ← w − η · m̂ / (√v̂ + ε)

Here m̂ = m / (1 − β₁ᵗ) and v̂ = v / (1 − β₂ᵗ) correct the bias from starting at zero. Defaults are β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.999 and ε = 10⁻⁸.

Dividing by √v̂ gives parameters with small or rare gradients relatively bigger steps, so Adam works well with little tuning and is the default for transformers. The cost is memory: two extra values per parameter, so the optimizer state takes twice the memory of the weights at the same precision.

Adding an L2 penalty to the gradient gets distorted by the adaptive scaling. AdamW fixes this by applying weight decay directly to the weights, and it is the version most people now use.
concepts.mixup: Adam and AdamW differ once weight decay is set. In plain Adam an L2 penalty is rescaled per parameter, so it regularizes unevenly. AdamW decouples the decay, which is why the same decay value behaves differently in the two.

concepts.name: Weight decay
concepts.summary: A regularizer that shrinks every weight a little toward zero on each update, which discourages large weights and overfitting.
concepts.body:
On each step the optimizer subtracts η·λ·w from each weight, where λ is the decay strength. That is the same as multiplying the weight by a factor just under 1. The model is pushed toward smaller, smoother solutions.

For plain SGD this is exactly the same as adding an L2 penalty (λ/2)‖w‖² to the loss. For adaptive optimizers like Adam it is not, because the L2 gradient gets divided by the adaptive scale. Decoupled weight decay, as in AdamW, applies the shrink directly to the weights and is the standard choice.

Common practice is to skip decay on biases and normalization parameters. As a rule of thumb, values with AdamW are around 0.01 to 0.1.

Example: with η = 0.001 and λ = 0.1, each step multiplies a weight by 1 − 0.0001 = 0.9999, alongside the usual gradient update.
concepts.mixup: Weight decay and L2 regularization are often treated as one thing. They match only for plain SGD. With Adam they diverge, so a value tuned for one setup does not transfer to the other.

concepts.name: Learning rate schedule
concepts.summary: A plan for changing the learning rate during training, usually a short warmup followed by a gradual decay.
concepts.body:
A fixed learning rate is rarely best. Early on, a high rate makes fast progress. Later, a lower rate lets the model settle into a good minimum instead of bouncing around it.

Common shapes:

- Warmup: raise the rate linearly from near zero over the first few hundred or thousand steps. Adam's variance estimates are unreliable at the start, and transformers often diverge without warmup.
- Cosine decay: follow half a cosine curve from the peak down to a small floor by the end of training.
- Step decay: cut the rate by a fixed factor, such as 10, at set epochs.
- Reduce on plateau: cut it when validation loss stops improving.

Example: warm up over 1,000 steps to a peak of 3×10⁻⁴, then decay along a cosine to 3×10⁻⁵ over the remaining 99,000 steps.

The schedule's length should match the real run. Stopping halfway through a cosine schedule leaves the model at a high rate.
concepts.mixup: Warmup is not the same as using a small learning rate throughout. It is a ramp that ends at a normal or even high peak. Its job is to avoid early instability, not to slow training down.

concepts.name: Batch size
concepts.summary: The number of examples used to compute one gradient estimate and one weight update.
concepts.body:
Each training step averages the gradient over a mini-batch. A bigger batch gives a less noisy estimate and uses the hardware more fully, so each epoch runs faster. But there are fewer updates per epoch, and past a point a bigger batch stops cutting the number of steps needed.

Batch size and learning rate move together. A common heuristic for SGD is to scale the learning rate linearly with batch size, with warmup. For Adam, square-root scaling is a common starting point. Very large batches can generalize a little worse unless tuned carefully, while small batches add noise that acts as mild regularization.

Memory sets the upper limit, since activations grow with batch size. Gradient accumulation reaches a larger effective batch on limited memory.

Example: a per-device batch of 16, 4 accumulation steps and 8 GPUs give an effective batch of 16 × 4 × 8 = 512.

At inference, batch size trades latency for throughput instead.
concepts.mixup: An epoch is one full pass over the data and a step is one batch. With 10,000 examples and a batch of 100, an epoch is 100 steps, so changing batch size changes how many updates an epoch contains.

concepts.name: Transfer learning
concepts.summary: Reusing a model trained on a large general task as the starting point for a new, usually smaller, task.
concepts.body:
A model pretrained on lots of data has already learned useful general features, such as edges and shapes for images, or grammar and meaning for text. Instead of starting from random weights, you start from those.

Two common modes:

- Feature extraction: freeze the pretrained layers and train only a new head on top. Fast and safe with little data.
- Fine-tuning: also update some or all pretrained layers, usually with a smaller learning rate so the useful features are not destroyed.

It matters because labelled data is expensive. With a few thousand labelled images, a fine-tuned pretrained network usually beats one trained from scratch by a wide margin.

Example: a clinic has 2,000 labelled skin images. Start from a network pretrained on a large photo dataset, replace its output layer with a 7-class layer, train the head first, then unfreeze the top blocks with a lower learning rate.

It works best when the source and target domains are related.
concepts.mixup: Transfer learning is the broad idea and fine-tuning is one way to do it. Freezing the backbone and training only a head is also transfer learning, and with tiny datasets it is often the safer choice.

concepts.name: Data augmentation
concepts.summary: Creating extra training examples by applying label-preserving changes, such as flips, crops or noise, to the data you already have.
concepts.body:
The model sees a slightly different version of each example every epoch, which teaches it which changes should not affect the answer. This reduces overfitting and improves robustness, especially with small datasets.

Common choices:

- Images: random crops, flips, small rotations, colour jitter, mixup and cutout.
- Audio: time shifts, added noise, speed changes, masking parts of a spectrogram.
- Text: back-translation, synonym swaps, or paraphrases generated by an LLM.

Each change must keep the label true. A horizontal flip is fine for cats but changes the meaning of a left-turn sign or of letters such as b and d. Augmentation is applied to the training set on the fly. Validation and test data stay unchanged so they reflect real inputs.

Example: a defect detector trained on 500 photos gets random rotations and brightness changes, so it copes with factory lighting that varies through the day.
concepts.mixup: Augmenting before splitting puts near-copies of the same example in both the training and test sets, which inflates test scores. Split first, then augment only the training part.

concepts.name: Embedding
concepts.summary: A learned dense vector that represents an item, such as a word, product or user, so that similar items sit close together.
concepts.body:
An embedding layer is a lookup table: a matrix with one row per item ID. A vocabulary of 50,000 tokens with 768-dimensional embeddings is a 50,000 × 768 matrix, about 38 million parameters. The rows are learned during training, so items used in similar ways end up with similar vectors.

Embeddings replace sparse one-hot vectors with short dense ones that carry meaning. They show up everywhere: token inputs to transformers, user and item vectors in recommenders, and sentence or document embeddings for semantic search and RAG, where a separate model maps a whole text to one vector.

Closeness is usually measured with cosine similarity or dot product. In a good text embedding space, 'refund my order' lands near 'I want my money back' even though they share no words.

Embeddings from different models live in different spaces and cannot be compared with each other.
concepts.mixup: Token embeddings and sentence embeddings are different things. Token embeddings are the input rows of a language model. Sentence embeddings come from a model trained, often contrastively, to make whole texts comparable. Averaging raw token vectors is usually a poor substitute.

concepts.name: Contrastive learning
concepts.summary: Learning embeddings by pulling matching pairs together and pushing non-matching pairs apart in vector space.
concepts.body:
You need pairs that should match, called positives: two augmented crops of the same photo, a question and its answer, an image and its caption. Other items act as negatives. The loss rewards high similarity for positives and low similarity for negatives.

The common InfoNCE loss treats it as classification. For an anchor a with positive p and negatives n₁ to nₖ, loss = −log( exp(s(a, p) / τ) / Σₓ exp(s(a, x) / τ) ), where the sum runs over p and all the negatives, s is cosine similarity and τ is a temperature. With in-batch negatives, every other item in the batch is a negative, so bigger batches give more negatives.

It is how most text and image embedding models for search and RAG are trained, and how image-text models learn a shared space. It needs no class labels, only a way to form positive pairs.

Hard negatives, items that look similar but do not match, teach the most.
concepts.mixup: Contrastive learning is not a classifier with many fixed classes. It learns a similarity space, so at test time it can compare items it never saw in training, which a fixed classifier cannot do.

concepts.name: Tokenization
concepts.summary: Splitting text into the units a language model actually reads, usually subword pieces from a fixed vocabulary, each mapped to an integer ID.
concepts.body:
Models do not see characters or words. A tokenizer maps text to a list of token IDs from a vocabulary of tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand entries. Most use subword methods such as byte-pair encoding (BPE), which starts from bytes or characters and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair. Common words become one token and rare words split into pieces, so no input is ever out of vocabulary.

Tokens are the unit of cost, latency and context limits. A common rule of thumb is that an English token averages about three quarters of a word, but code, numbers and many non-English languages need more tokens for the same content. Tokenization also explains odd failures such as miscounting the letters in a word, since the model sees chunks rather than letters.

Example: 'unbelievable' might become 'un', 'believ' and 'able'. A tokenizer must match its model exactly, since the IDs mean nothing to any other model.
concepts.mixup: Token counts are not word counts. In English, tokens usually run about a third higher than words, and far higher for code or languages the tokenizer was not built around. Budgeting context or cost by words underestimates both.

concepts.name: Self-attention
concepts.summary: A layer where each token builds its new representation as a weighted mix of all tokens' values, with weights set by query-key similarity.
concepts.body:
Each token's vector is projected into a query q, a key k and a value v using learned matrices. Stacked for all tokens:

Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵀ / √d_k) V

Row i of QKᵀ scores how relevant every token is to token i. Softmax turns the scores into weights that sum to 1, and the output is the weighted sum of value vectors. Dividing by √d_k stops the scores growing with dimension, which would push softmax toward a near one-hot output with tiny gradients.

Any token can draw information directly from any other in one step, unlike an RNN, and all positions are computed in parallel. The cost is that the score matrix is n × n, so compute and memory grow with the square of sequence length.

Example: in 'the trophy did not fit in the case because it was too big', attention lets 'it' put a high weight on 'trophy'.
concepts.mixup: Self-attention on its own has no sense of order. Shuffle the input tokens and the outputs are simply shuffled the same way. Position information has to be added separately, through positional encodings.

concepts.name: Multi-head attention
concepts.summary: Running several attention operations in parallel on smaller projections, so each head can focus on a different kind of relationship.
concepts.body:
Instead of one attention over the full model width d, the model splits it into h heads of size d / h. Each head has its own query, key and value projections and computes attention independently. The head outputs are concatenated back to width d and passed through an output projection.

The total compute is about the same as one full-width attention, but the model gets h separate attention patterns. In trained models some heads track nearby tokens, some follow syntax and some copy earlier text, although many heads are redundant and can be pruned.

Example: with d = 768 and 12 heads, each head works in 64 dimensions. The query, key, value and output projections are each 768 × 768, so one attention layer has about 4 × 768² ≈ 2.4 million weights, plus biases if used.

At inference every head's keys and values must be cached, which is why variants such as grouped-query attention share keys and values across heads.
concepts.mixup: More heads do not mean more parameters. The width is split across heads, so 8 or 16 heads at the same model width cost about the same. What changes is how many separate attention patterns the layer can form.

concepts.name: Causal mask
concepts.summary: A mask that stops each token from attending to later tokens, so a model learning to predict the next token cannot peek at it.
concepts.body:
Before the softmax in self-attention, every score where the key position comes after the query position is set to −∞. After softmax those weights become exactly zero. The allowed region is the lower triangle of the n × n score matrix, so token i sees only tokens 1 to i.

This makes decoder-only training efficient. One forward pass over a sequence of length n gives n next-token predictions at once, each using only the past, which matches what the model will have at generation time. Without the mask the model would learn to copy the next token and fail when generating.

It also makes caching possible. Earlier tokens never depend on later ones, so their keys and values can be stored and reused as new tokens are added.

Example: for 'the cat sat', the prediction made at 'cat' can use 'the' and 'cat' but never 'sat'.
concepts.mixup: A causal mask and a padding mask do different jobs. The padding mask hides filler tokens added to make sequences in a batch the same length. The causal mask hides the future. Batched decoder training usually applies both.

concepts.name: Positional encoding
concepts.summary: Information about each token's position added to a transformer, because attention by itself ignores word order.
concepts.body:
Attention treats its input as a set, so 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' would look the same without a position signal. The main approaches:

- Sinusoidal: add fixed sine and cosine waves of different frequencies to each token embedding. Used in the original transformer.
- Learned absolute: add a trained vector per position. Simple, but it cannot handle positions beyond the trained maximum.
- Rotary (RoPE): rotate the query and key vectors by an angle that depends on position, so their dot product depends on the distance between the tokens. Widely used in modern LLMs.
- ALiBi: add a penalty to attention scores that grows with distance.

Position handling is central to long-context work. Extending a model beyond its training length usually means rescaling RoPE frequencies and then fine-tuning on longer sequences.

Example: with RoPE, the positional effect between tokens 5 and 8 is the same as between tokens 105 and 108, since only the gap of 3 matters.
concepts.mixup: Absolute encodings tell the model where a token sits. Relative methods such as RoPE tell attention how far apart two tokens are. Relative methods cope better when the same text appears at different positions, which is one reason they are widely used.

concepts.name: Transformer block
concepts.summary: The repeated unit of a transformer: self-attention then a feed-forward network, each wrapped in normalization and a residual connection.
concepts.body:
A transformer is a stack of identical blocks. In the common pre-norm form, each block computes:

- h = x + Attention(Norm(x))
- out = h + FFN(Norm(h))

Attention mixes information across tokens. The feed-forward network (FFN) is an MLP applied to each token separately, usually expanding the width about 4× and projecting back. Gated versions such as SwiGLU use three matrices with a smaller expansion, about 8/3×, which keeps a similar parameter count. The residual connections keep gradients flowing through dozens of layers, and the norms keep activations stable.

In a standard design the attention weights take about 4d² and the FFN about 8d², so the FFN holds about two thirds of each block.

Example: with d = 1,024, one block has about 4 × 1,024² ≈ 4.2 million attention weights and 8 × 1,024² ≈ 8.4 million FFN weights, about 12.6 million in total. A 24-layer model then has roughly 300 million block parameters, before embeddings.
concepts.mixup: Attention gets the attention, but it is not where most of the weights are. The feed-forward layers hold most of the parameters, and they are where mixture-of-experts designs add capacity.
