concepts.name: Agent memory
concepts.summary: How an agent keeps information beyond one model call: the working history in its context, plus longer-term stores it can save to and read from.
concepts.body:
A model has no memory between calls. Everything it should know must be in the context window each time. Agents build memory on top of that:
- **Short-term or working memory**: the current conversation and tool results, kept in context. When it grows too long, older parts are summarized or dropped.
- **Long-term memory**: facts saved outside the model, such as user preferences, past decisions or notes on a long task, kept in files, a database or a vector store and retrieved when relevant.

The hard parts are deciding what is worth saving, keeping it correct when facts change, and retrieving the right piece later without flooding the context.

Example: a travel assistant saves "prefers aisle seats and vegetarian meals" after one chat. A month later it retrieves that note while booking and does not ask again.

Memory carries risk too. A wrong or injected memory persists and is trusted in later sessions, and stored personal data needs consent and deletion rules.
concepts.mixup: A long context window is not memory. It resets every session, and stuffing everything into it raises cost and can bury the details that matter. Memory means deciding what to keep and what to recall.

concepts.name: Context engineering
concepts.summary: Deciding what information goes into a model's context window at each step, and in what form, so it has what it needs and little else.
concepts.body:
Context engineering widens prompt engineering from wording one prompt to managing everything the model sees across many steps: system instructions, tool definitions, retrieved documents, memory, conversation history and tool results.

It matters because context is limited and costs money, and models tend to use information less reliably as the context grows long and cluttered. Irrelevant text distracts, and details buried in the middle of a long context can be missed.

Common techniques:
- Retrieve information just in time instead of loading everything up front.
- Trim or summarize old tool results, keeping IDs and conclusions. This is often called compaction.
- Let the agent keep notes in a file it can re-read.
- Give sub-agents clean contexts and take back only their summaries.

Example: after 40 steps, an agent's context holds 120,000 tokens, mostly raw logs it has already read. Replacing those logs with a 2,000-token summary of findings keeps the key facts and frees room for the next steps.
concepts.mixup: Context engineering is not filling the biggest window you can. More context can make answers worse. The skill is choosing the smallest set of high-value information for the step at hand.

concepts.name: Human in the loop
concepts.summary: Building points into an AI system where a person reviews, approves, corrects or takes over before or after the system acts.
concepts.body:
Not every decision should be fully automated. Human-in-the-loop design puts a person at the points where a mistake is costly, hard to undo or legally sensitive.

Common forms:
- **Approval gates**: the agent proposes an action, such as sending money or deleting data, and waits for a yes.
- **Confidence routing**: low-confidence predictions go to a review queue.
- **Escalation**: a bot hands the conversation to a person.
- **Feedback**: human corrections become labels for evaluation and training.

The design questions are which actions need approval, what the reviewer sees so they can judge quickly, and how many cases the review team can actually handle.

Example: an insurance claims model auto-approves claims under $500 when its confidence is above 0.95. Everything else, about 15% of claims, goes to an adjuster along with the model's reasons.

Watch for automation bias. Reviewers who approve 99% of items start clicking yes without reading.
concepts.mixup: Adding a human does not make a system safe on its own. If the reviewer lacks the context, time or authority to disagree, the approval is a rubber stamp. Track how often reviewers override the system.

concepts.name: Least privilege
concepts.summary: Give an agent, tool or service only the permissions it needs for its task, so a mistake or an attack can do only limited harm.
concepts.body:
An agent's real power is the sum of its tools and credentials. If it is fooled by prompt injection or simply makes an error, it can do anything those permissions allow. Least privilege shrinks that blast radius.

In practice:
- Read-only access unless writing is truly needed.
- Narrow tools such as `refund_order(order_id, amount)` with a coded cap on the amount, instead of raw database or payment access.
- Credentials scoped to the current user and tenant, not a shared admin key.
- Short-lived tokens and a separate identity per agent, so actions can be audited.
- Network and file access limited to what the task uses.

Example: a support agent that answers order questions gets read access to the signed-in customer's orders only. A message that tells it to export every customer's email address fails, because no tool it holds can reach that data.

Enforce these limits in code and infrastructure, not in the system prompt.
concepts.mixup: Telling the model "never access other users' data" in its prompt is not least privilege. Prompts can be overridden. Real limits live in the permissions of the credentials and tools, where the model cannot talk its way past them.

concepts.name: Sandboxing
concepts.summary: Running untrusted actions, such as code a model wrote, in an isolated environment that limits what they can read, change or reach.
concepts.body:
Agents often run code or shell commands that a model wrote. That code might be buggy, or steered by injected instructions. A sandbox runs it where damage cannot spread.

Typical limits:
- Isolation through containers, lightweight virtual machines or WebAssembly runtimes, with a separate filesystem.
- No network access, or only an allow list of hosts.
- No secrets or production credentials inside.
- CPU, memory and time caps, so an endless loop gets killed.
- A fresh, throwaway environment for each task.

Example: a data analysis agent writes Python to read an uploaded CSV. It runs in a container with only that file mounted, no network and a 60-second limit. If the code tries to read `~/.ssh` or contact an outside server, it simply fails.

Sandboxing pairs with least privilege. One limits where the code runs, and the other limits which credentials and tools it holds.
concepts.mixup: A plain container is not always a strong boundary. Containers share the host's kernel, so for code that may be truly hostile, teams often add stronger isolation such as lightweight virtual machines. Match the isolation to the threat.

concepts.name: Idempotency
concepts.summary: An operation is idempotent if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once, which makes retries safe.
concepts.body:
Networks fail in ways where you cannot tell whether a request went through. The call may have succeeded and only the reply was lost. Retry a non-idempotent action such as "charge $50" and the customer may pay twice.

Common ways to make actions idempotent:
- **Idempotency keys**: the client sends a unique ID with the request and the server records it. A repeat with the same key returns the first result instead of acting again.
- **Set, not add**: `set balance = 100` is idempotent, `add 10 to balance` is not.
- **Check before acting**: create the ticket only if none exists with this external ID.

This matters for agents because they retry, repeat steps after errors, and sometimes call the same tool twice by mistake.

Example: an agent calls `issue_refund(order_id=812, key="r-812-1")`, the call times out, and it retries. The payment service sees key r-812-1 again and returns the original refund instead of paying out a second time.
concepts.mixup: Idempotent does not mean read-only. Deleting one record changes state, but deleting it again changes nothing more, so it is idempotent. Every read-only call is idempotent, but not every idempotent call is read-only.

concepts.name: Trajectory evaluation
concepts.summary: Judging an agent on the path it took, its sequence of steps and tool calls, not only on whether the final answer was right.
concepts.body:
An agent can reach the right answer by a bad path, with 30 wasted calls, a risky action or plain luck. It can also follow a sensible path and stumble at the last step. Looking only at the final output hides both.

Trajectory evaluation inspects the full trace. Typical checks:
- Did it call the required tools, with valid arguments?
- Did it avoid forbidden actions, such as deleting data?
- How many steps, tokens and seconds did it use?
- Did it recover from tool errors?
- Does the sequence match a reference path, exactly, in order, or as a set of required steps?

The outcome still matters most. Many valid paths can solve a task, so demanding one exact path punishes good alternatives.

Example: two agent versions both solve 85 of 100 tasks. Version B averages 6 tool calls against A's 14 and never calls `delete_record`. The traces show B is clearly the better choice, which the success rate alone could not.
concepts.mixup: Matching a reference trajectory step by step is not the goal. Agents often find valid alternative routes. Score the outcome and the hard constraints, and use step-level comparisons to diagnose failures rather than as the only grade.

concepts.name: Compounding errors
concepts.summary: In a multi-step agent, small per-step error rates multiply, so the chance of finishing a long task with no mistakes falls quickly.
concepts.body:
If each step succeeds independently with probability p, a task of n steps succeeds with probability pⁿ.

Example: at 95% per step, a 10-step task succeeds 0.95¹⁰ ≈ 0.60 of the time, and a 30-step task only 0.95³⁰ ≈ 0.21. A step accuracy that sounds high still fails most long tasks.

Errors also feed forward. A wrong value fetched at step 2 becomes an input to every later step, and the agent may build on it confidently.

Ways to fight it:
- Fewer steps: better tools that do more per call, or fixed workflows for the known parts.
- Checks between steps: validate outputs, run tests, verify against sources.
- Recovery: let the agent notice failures and retry or re-plan.
- Human checkpoints before costly or hard-to-undo steps.

Independence is a simplification. Real errors can cluster, and a step that catches and fixes an earlier mistake breaks the chain. But the pⁿ picture explains why step reliability matters so much.
concepts.mixup: Per-step accuracy is not task accuracy. A demo where each step looks right 95% of the time can still fail most real 30-step tasks. Measure success on whole tasks, not just single steps.

concepts.name: Quantization
concepts.summary: Storing a model's weights, and sometimes its activations, with fewer bits, such as 8 or 4 instead of 16, to cut memory and speed up inference.
concepts.body:
Quantization maps high-precision numbers onto a small grid of levels. A common scheme uses a scale s and a zero point z: q = round(x / s) + z, and the value comes back as x ≈ s × (q − z). Post-training quantization (PTQ) converts a trained model using a small calibration set. Quantization-aware training (QAT) simulates the rounding during training so the model learns to tolerate it.

It matters because LLM serving is often limited by memory size and memory bandwidth. Fewer bytes per weight means a bigger model fits on one GPU and each decode step reads less data.

Example: a 7B-parameter model needs 7 × 10⁹ × 2 bytes = 14 GB of weights in FP16, 7 GB in INT8 and about 3.5 GB in 4-bit, before the KV cache and activations. Quality usually suffers first from outlier values and very low bit widths, so rerun your evals after quantizing.
concepts.mixup: Weight-only quantization saves memory and speeds up memory-bound decoding, but the maths often still runs in 16-bit after the weights are unpacked. Faster compute needs the activations quantized too, plus hardware kernels for that format. Quantization is also different from mixed precision training, which keeps a full-precision master copy.

concepts.name: Knowledge distillation
concepts.summary: Training a small student model to copy the outputs of a larger teacher model, so it keeps much of the quality at a fraction of the cost.
concepts.body:
The student learns from the teacher's soft outputs, not only the hard labels. The classic loss mixes cross-entropy on the true labels with a term that pulls the student's probabilities toward the teacher's, both softened by a temperature T:

loss = α × CE(y, student) + (1 − α) × T² × KL(teacher_T ‖ student_T)

Soft targets carry extra information, such as which wrong classes the teacher finds similar. The T² factor keeps the soft term's gradients at a sensible size as T grows.

For LLMs, a common form is to let the teacher generate answers and fine-tune the student on them, sometimes called sequence-level distillation.

Example: a support bot runs on a large model that costs too much per query. You run the large model on 200,000 real tickets, fine-tune a small model on its replies and serve the small model, keeping the large one for the hardest cases.
concepts.mixup: Distillation trains a new, smaller model. Quantization and pruning shrink the same model in place. They stack well: a distilled student can then be quantized. Distillation also needs the teacher's outputs, not just a copy of its weights.

concepts.name: Pruning
concepts.summary: Removing weights, neurons, attention heads or whole layers that contribute little, to make a model smaller and sometimes faster.
concepts.body:
The simplest method is magnitude pruning: set the smallest weights to zero, then fine-tune briefly to recover accuracy. Unstructured pruning zeroes single weights anywhere in a matrix. Structured pruning removes whole units such as channels, attention heads or layers.

The difference matters in practice. Unstructured sparsity shrinks the model on paper, but dense GPU kernels still do the same work unless the hardware supports that sparse pattern, such as 2:4 sparsity, where 2 of every 4 weights are zero. Structured pruning gives real speedups on ordinary hardware because the matrices really get smaller.

Example: pruning 50% of the weights of a 100M-parameter model leaves 50M nonzero weights. Stored as a dense matrix, it still uses the same memory and time. Remove half the channels of each layer instead and the matrix multiplies themselves shrink, so the model runs faster.
concepts.mixup: A high sparsity figure does not mean a matching speedup. Unless the zeros fall in a pattern the hardware or a sparse kernel can skip, a 90% sparse model can run just as slowly as the dense one.

concepts.name: Mixed precision training
concepts.summary: Training with 16-bit numbers for most of the maths while keeping sensitive parts, such as a master copy of the weights, in 32-bit for stability.
concepts.body:
Most matrix multiplies run in FP16 or BF16, which halves activation memory and uses the GPU's fast tensor cores. Numerically sensitive steps, such as the weight update, large sums and softmax, stay in FP32, and the optimizer keeps FP32 master weights.

The two 16-bit formats differ. FP16 has 5 exponent bits, so small gradients can underflow to zero. Loss scaling fixes this: multiply the loss by a factor such as 1,024 before backprop, divide the gradients by it before the update, and skip any step that overflows. BF16 has 8 exponent bits, the same range as FP32, so it usually needs no loss scaling but has less precision.

Example: Adam with mixed precision stores about 16 bytes per parameter: 2 for 16-bit weights, 2 for gradients, 4 for FP32 master weights and 8 for the two Adam moments. A 1B-parameter model needs about 16 GB before activations.
concepts.mixup: Mixed precision does not shrink the memory for weights, gradients and optimizer state. With Adam it is about 16 bytes per parameter either way. The savings come from smaller activations and much faster tensor core maths. It is also different from quantizing a model for inference.

concepts.name: Gradient checkpointing
concepts.summary: Saving training memory by keeping only some activations from the forward pass and recomputing the rest during the backward pass.
concepts.body:
Backprop needs the activations from the forward pass. Normally all of them stay in memory, and with long sequences or big batches they can take more memory than the weights. With checkpointing you store activations only at chosen points, such as the input to each transformer block, and rerun the forward pass of a block when its gradients are needed.

The trade is compute for memory. Recomputing costs about one extra forward pass. Using the rule of thumb that a backward pass costs about twice a forward pass, a step goes from about 3 units of work to 4, roughly a third more.

Example: a 24-layer model uses 1 GB of activations per block at your batch size, 24 GB in total. Suppose each block's input is 0.1 GB. Checkpointing every block keeps 24 × 0.1 = 2.4 GB of inputs plus about 1 GB for the block being recomputed, about 3.4 GB. The freed memory can hold a much bigger batch.
concepts.mixup: Gradient checkpointing has nothing to do with saving model checkpoints to disk. It also saves only activation memory, not the memory for weights, gradients or optimizer state, which needs sharding or lower precision instead.

concepts.name: Gradient accumulation
concepts.summary: Running several small micro-batches and adding up their gradients before one optimizer step, to train with a large effective batch that would not fit in memory.
concepts.body:
Instead of stepping the optimizer after every batch, you run forward and backward on k micro-batches, let the gradients add up, then take one step and reset them.

Effective batch size = micro-batch size × accumulation steps × number of GPUs.

It is used when the batch size you want for stable training does not fit in GPU memory. It costs time, not memory: k micro-batches take about as long as k normal steps.

Example: you want a batch of 256, only 32 fit per GPU, and you have 2 GPUs. Accumulate over 4 steps: 32 × 4 × 2 = 256.

Two details matter. Scale each micro-batch loss by 1/k, or the summed gradient is k times too large, which acts like a bigger learning rate. And batch normalization still sees only the micro-batch, so its statistics do not match a true large batch.
concepts.mixup: Gradient accumulation matches a large batch for the gradient, but it does not make training faster. It is also different from gradient checkpointing, which trades extra compute for less activation memory inside a single step.

concepts.name: KV cache
concepts.summary: During generation, storing each earlier token's attention keys and values so every new token computes only its own, instead of reprocessing the whole sequence.
concepts.body:
In a decoder, each new token attends to all earlier tokens through their keys and values. These never change once computed, so the model caches them. Each decode step then runs the model on just the new token and reads the rest from the cache.

The cost is memory, which grows with sequence length and batch size:

KV bytes = 2 × layers × KV heads × head dim × tokens × batch × bytes per value

The 2 counts keys and values.

Example: 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head dim 128, FP16 (2 bytes). Per token that is 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 131,072 bytes, about 0.13 MB. A 4,096-token sequence needs about 0.54 GB, and a batch of 16 such sequences about 8.6 GB (1 GB = 10⁹ bytes). That memory, not compute, often caps how many requests a GPU can serve at once.
concepts.mixup: The KV cache works within one generation, across decode steps. Prompt caching is different: it reuses the cache of a shared prefix across separate requests. Semantic caching is different again, since it reuses whole answers for similar questions.

concepts.name: Continuous batching
concepts.summary: An LLM serving method that adds and removes requests from the running batch at every decode step, instead of waiting for the whole batch to finish.
concepts.body:
With static batching, a group of requests starts together and the GPU keeps going until the longest reply is done. Short replies finish early and their slots sit idle. Continuous batching schedules at the level of single decode steps. When a sequence emits its end token it leaves the batch, and a waiting request takes its slot at the next step.

This keeps the GPU busy and can raise throughput several times when reply lengths vary. It needs careful KV cache memory management, since sequences of different lengths come and go, which is why it is usually paired with paged allocation of the KV cache.

Example: a batch of 8 has replies from 50 to 800 tokens long. Under static batching, the slots of the short replies sit idle until the 800-token reply finishes. Continuous batching fills each freed slot with a new request straight away.
concepts.mixup: Dynamic batching, which waits a few milliseconds to group incoming requests, still runs each group to completion. Continuous batching changes the batch at every step. Also, packing more requests in raises total throughput but can slow each step a little, so per-user speed may drop.

concepts.name: Speculative decoding
concepts.summary: Speeding up generation by letting a small draft model propose several tokens, then having the large model check them all in one forward pass.
concepts.body:
Decoding is slow because the big model makes one token per pass and each pass is limited by reading its weights from memory. In speculative decoding a cheap draft model guesses the next k tokens. The target model then scores all k positions in a single pass, which takes about as long as one normal step. It accepts drafted tokens in order until one fails its check, then supplies one token of its own.

With greedy decoding the check is simply whether the target would pick the same token. With sampling, a rejection-sampling rule keeps the output distribution exactly the target model's. Quality does not change, only speed.

Example: the draft proposes 4 tokens. The target accepts the first 3, rejects the 4th and puts its own token there. One large-model pass produced 4 tokens instead of 1. If drafts are usually rejected, you pay for the draft model and gain little.
concepts.mixup: Speculative decoding is not an approximation like quantization or distillation. The big model still decides every token, so outputs follow its distribution. The speedup depends on the acceptance rate, so it helps most on predictable text such as code or templated replies.

concepts.name: FlashAttention
concepts.summary: An exact attention algorithm that works through the computation in tiles held in fast on-chip memory, so the full N × N score matrix is never written to GPU main memory.
concepts.body:
Standard attention computes the score matrix QKᵀ, writes it to the GPU's high-bandwidth memory (HBM), reads it back for softmax, writes again, then multiplies by V. For N tokens that matrix has N² entries, so memory use and memory traffic grow quadratically.

FlashAttention splits Q, K and V into blocks that fit in on-chip SRAM. An online softmax keeps a running maximum and sum, so partial results from each block can be combined exactly. In the backward pass it recomputes the scores instead of storing them.

The output is the same as standard attention, but extra memory grows only linearly with N and far less data moves, which makes long contexts practical and training faster.

Example: at N = 8,192 tokens, one head's score matrix has about 67 million entries, about 134 MB in FP16, for each head in each layer. FlashAttention never stores it.
concepts.mixup: FlashAttention is exact, not an approximation like sparse or linear attention. It still does O(N²) arithmetic. It is faster because it cuts reads and writes to slow memory, not because it does fewer FLOPs.

concepts.name: Grouped-query attention
concepts.summary: An attention variant where groups of query heads share one key head and one value head, which shrinks the KV cache with little loss in quality.
concepts.body:
In standard multi-head attention (MHA), every query head has its own key and value heads. Multi-query attention (MQA) goes to the other extreme: all query heads share a single key head and value head. Grouped-query attention sits in between. With H query heads and G key-value groups, each group of H / G query heads shares one key-value pair.

It matters because decoding is limited by reading the KV cache, and the cache size is proportional to the number of KV heads. Fewer KV heads means less memory per token, so longer contexts and bigger batches fit.

Example: a model with 32 query heads and 8 KV heads has a KV cache 32 / 8 = 4 times smaller than the same model with full multi-head attention. MQA, with 1 KV head, would make it 32 times smaller but tends to lose more quality.
concepts.mixup: GQA keeps all the query heads, so it is not the same as using fewer attention heads. What shrinks is the number of stored key and value heads. G = H gives ordinary multi-head attention and G = 1 gives multi-query attention.

concepts.name: Data parallelism
concepts.summary: Training on many GPUs by giving each one a full copy of the model and a different slice of the batch, then averaging gradients before every update.
concepts.body:
Each GPU, or worker, holds the same weights, runs forward and backward on its own shard of the data and computes local gradients. An all-reduce operation then averages the gradients across workers, so every copy takes the same update and stays in sync. To save time, the all-reduce is overlapped with the backward pass.

It is the simplest way to scale training and works well when the model fits on one GPU. The global batch grows with the number of workers, so the learning rate and warmup may need retuning.

Example: 8 GPUs with a batch of 32 each give a global batch of 256. Each step handles 8 times the data in about the time one GPU takes for 32 examples, plus the all-reduce cost.

Its limit is memory, because every GPU stores the full weights, gradients and optimizer state.
concepts.mixup: Data parallelism splits the data, model parallelism splits the model. If the model does not fit on one GPU, plain data parallelism cannot help, and you need sharded data parallelism or model parallelism.

concepts.name: Model parallelism
concepts.summary: Splitting one model across several GPUs, by layers or within layers, so a model too big for one device can be trained or served.
concepts.body:
There are two main kinds. Pipeline parallelism puts different layers on different GPUs, like stations on an assembly line. To keep every stage busy, the batch is cut into micro-batches that flow through in turn. Some idle time, called the pipeline bubble, remains at the start and end of each batch.

Tensor parallelism splits single weight matrices across GPUs, so each computes part of every layer's matrix multiply and they exchange results inside each layer. This needs very fast links between GPUs, so it usually stays within one server.

Large training runs often combine tensor, pipeline and data parallelism.

Example: an 80B-parameter model needs 80 × 10⁹ × 2 bytes = 160 GB for its FP16 weights, so it cannot fit on one 80 GB GPU. Tensor parallelism across 4 GPUs puts 40 GB of weights on each, leaving room for the KV cache.
concepts.mixup: Model parallelism splits the model, while data parallelism copies the model and splits the batch. Naive pipeline parallelism without micro-batches leaves all but one GPU idle at any moment, so it gives more total memory but no speedup.

concepts.name: Sharded data parallelism
concepts.summary: Data parallelism where each GPU stores only a slice of the weights, gradients and optimizer state, gathering a layer's full weights only while that layer runs.
concepts.body:
In plain data parallelism every GPU holds a full copy of everything, which wastes memory. Sharded data parallelism splits these across the N GPUs. The ZeRO stages describe how far it goes: stage 1 shards the optimizer state, stage 2 also shards gradients and stage 3 also shards the weights. Fully sharded data parallel (FSDP) works in the stage 3 style.

Before computing a layer, the GPUs all-gather its weights, use them, then free them. Gradients are reduce-scattered so each GPU keeps only its own slice. You pay extra communication to save memory.

Example: mixed-precision Adam needs about 16 bytes per parameter, so a 7B model needs about 7 × 16 = 112 GB, which does not fit on one 80 GB GPU. Fully sharded across 8 GPUs, that is about 14 GB each, leaving room for activations.
concepts.mixup: Sharded data parallelism is still data parallelism. Each GPU processes its own data and runs every layer in full, holding the complete weights only briefly. Tensor parallelism instead splits the maths of each layer across GPUs.

concepts.name: Throughput vs latency
concepts.summary: Latency is how long one request takes, while throughput is how many requests or tokens the system finishes per second, and raising one often hurts the other.
concepts.body:
In model serving the main lever is batching. Bigger batches use the GPU better, so total tokens per second rise. But each request may wait to join a batch and each step takes a little longer, so per-request latency rises.

LLM serving uses finer measures: time to first token (TTFT), time per output token (TPOT), end-to-end latency, and total output tokens per second. Latency is reported as percentiles such as p50 and p99, because averages hide slow tail requests.

Example: at batch size 1 a GPU takes 50 ms per decode step, which is 20 tokens per second. At batch 32 each step takes 80 ms. Each user now gets 1 / 0.08 = 12.5 tokens per second, but the GPU produces 32 / 0.08 = 400 tokens per second in total.

The product picks the operating point: a chat app needs low latency, an overnight scoring job wants maximum throughput.
concepts.mixup: High throughput does not mean fast responses. A system can serve many tokens per second overall while each user waits longer. Little's law links them: average requests in flight = throughput × average latency.

concepts.name: Time to first token
concepts.summary: The delay between sending a request to an LLM and receiving its first generated token, the main measure of how responsive a streaming app feels.
concepts.body:
TTFT covers queueing, network time and the prefill phase, where the model processes the whole prompt in one pass and builds the KV cache. Prefill is compute-bound and grows with prompt length, so long prompts mean a long TTFT. After the first token, speed is measured as time per output token (TPOT), also called inter-token latency.

End-to-end latency ≈ TTFT + TPOT × (output tokens − 1)

Example: a RAG prompt of 6,000 tokens gives a TTFT of 600 ms, then the model streams at 25 ms per token. A 200-token answer takes about 0.6 + 0.025 × 199 ≈ 5.6 seconds in total, but the user starts reading after 0.6 seconds.

Ways to cut TTFT include shorter prompts, prompt caching for shared prefixes, and enough serving capacity that requests do not wait in a queue.
concepts.mixup: TTFT and total latency answer different questions. Streaming makes a reply feel faster but does not make it finish sooner. A long prompt mostly hurts TTFT, while a long answer mostly hurts total time.

concepts.name: Memory-bound decoding
concepts.summary: LLM token generation is usually limited by how fast the GPU can read weights and the KV cache from memory, not by how fast it can do arithmetic.
concepts.body:
Each decode step makes one new token per sequence but must read every weight once. At batch size 1 that is about 2 FLOPs per weight, roughly 1 FLOP per byte in FP16, while a modern GPU needs on the order of 100 or more FLOPs per byte to keep its compute units busy. This ratio of FLOPs to bytes moved is called arithmetic intensity. Prefill handles many tokens per weight read, so it is compute-bound. Decode is memory-bound.

A quick bound: time per step ≥ bytes read / memory bandwidth.

Example: a 7B model in FP16 has 14 GB of weights. On a GPU with 2 TB/s of bandwidth, one step needs at least 14 / 2,000 = 7 ms, so one sequence tops out near 140 tokens per second.

This explains the main serving tricks. Batching reuses each weight read across sequences, quantization reads fewer bytes, GQA shrinks the KV cache and speculative decoding checks several tokens per read.
concepts.mixup: A faster GPU in FLOPs barely helps small-batch decoding, because memory bandwidth is the limit. Prefill and decode also behave differently: processing a long prompt is compute-bound, while generating tokens one at a time is memory-bound.

concepts.name: Data drift
concepts.summary: A change over time in the distribution of a model's input features compared with the data it was trained on.
concepts.body:
Data drift means P(X) changes. Users, products, sensors or upstream pipelines change, and the inputs the model sees in production stop looking like the training set. The model may then be asked about regions it saw little of, and performance can fall.

Teams detect it by comparing recent production data with a reference window, usually the training data or a stable recent period, one feature at a time. Common tools are the population stability index (PSI), the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test for numeric features and the chi-squared test for categories. Watching the distribution of predictions helps too.

Example: a loan model was trained when most applicants were 30 to 50. A new campaign brings in many applicants aged 20 to 25. The age distribution has drifted, even if the link between age and default has not.

Drift is a warning, not proof of harm. Confirm with labelled performance where you can.
concepts.mixup: Data drift is a change in the inputs, P(X). Concept drift is a change in the relationship between inputs and the target, P(y | X). Data drift can be seen without labels, while concept drift usually needs labels to confirm.

concepts.name: Concept drift
concepts.summary: A change over time in the relationship between inputs and the target, so the same inputs now lead to different outcomes and the model's learned mapping goes stale.
concepts.body:
Concept drift means P(y | X) changes. The features may look exactly as before, but what they predict has moved. It can be sudden, such as a new fraud tactic, gradual, such as slowly changing tastes, or seasonal and recurring.

Because inputs can look unchanged, input drift checks may miss it. The reliable signal is falling performance on fresh labelled data, which is why label delay matters so much. Proxy signals such as rising complaints, more chargebacks or a shift in prediction scores can give earlier hints.

Example: a demand model learned that restaurants near offices are busy at lunch on weekdays. When many firms move to remote work, those lunches fall. The inputs, such as location, weekday and time, look the same, but the right answer for them has changed. The usual fix is retraining on recent data, sometimes with older data down-weighted.
concepts.mixup: People often call any drift concept drift. If only the mix of inputs changed, that is data drift, and the model may still be right wherever it has data. Concept drift means the true answer for the same input has changed.

concepts.name: Training-serving skew
concepts.summary: A difference between how features are computed, or what data looks like, in training and in production, which makes a model do worse live than it did offline.
concepts.body:
The model learns from features built one way, then sees features built another way. Common causes are separate code paths, such as a batch SQL job for training and a hand-written service for serving. Others are different defaults for missing values, unit or timezone mismatches, stale lookups at serving time, and training features that accidentally used information not available at prediction time.

It matters because offline metrics look fine while live results quietly suffer, and nothing crashes.

Example: in training, `days_since_last_order` is computed in UTC from the warehouse and missing values become 0. The serving code computes it in local time and returns −1 when missing. The model now sees values it never learned from.

Prevent it by sharing one feature definition for both paths, often through a feature store, by logging the features actually used at serving time and training on those logs, and by comparing training and serving feature distributions.
concepts.mixup: Skew is a mismatch built into the pipeline, present from day one. Drift is the world changing after launch. Both lower live performance, but skew is fixed in code, while drift is handled by retraining.

concepts.name: Feature store
concepts.summary: A system that defines, computes and stores ML features once, then serves the same values for building training sets and for low-latency online prediction.
concepts.body:
A feature store usually has two parts. The offline store keeps the full history of feature values, often in a data warehouse, for building training sets. The online store keeps the latest value for each entity, such as each user or card, in a fast key-value database for serving in milliseconds. One feature definition feeds both.

It solves three common problems. It cuts training-serving skew, because both paths use the same logic. It gives point-in-time correct training data, joining each label with the feature values as they were at that moment, which prevents leakage. And it lets teams reuse features instead of rebuilding them.

Example: a fraud model needs `card_txn_count_1h`. A streaming job keeps it fresh in the online store for every card. When building training data, the store returns each past transaction's value as of that transaction's timestamp, not today's value.

It is extra infrastructure, so a small team with one model may not need one.
concepts.mixup: A feature store is more than a table of features. Its value is point-in-time correct historical joins plus matching online values. Keeping only current values and joining them to old labels leaks future information into training.

concepts.name: Model registry
concepts.summary: A central record of trained model versions with their files, metadata and lifecycle stage, used to control which version is deployed.
concepts.body:
Each registered version links the model file to how it was made: the training data version, code commit, hyperparameters, evaluation results and owner. Versions move through stages such as candidate, staging, production and archived, often with an approval step.

Without a registry, nobody can quickly answer "which model is live, and how was it trained?" With one, deploying or rolling back means pointing serving at a different version, and there is an audit trail for regulated settings.

Example: version 14 of a churn model is in production. Version 15 passes offline checks and is registered as a candidate. After a canary release it is promoted to production, and version 14 is kept, so rolling back is one step.
concepts.mixup: A model registry is not an experiment tracker. The tracker logs every training run, most of which are thrown away. The registry holds the few chosen models that may be deployed, with their status and lineage.

concepts.name: Reproducibility
concepts.summary: Being able to rebuild the same model, or explain any difference, from recorded code, data, configuration and environment.
concepts.body:
To reproduce a model you need to pin four things: the code version, the exact data snapshot, the configuration including hyperparameters and random seeds, and the environment, meaning library versions and hardware.

It matters for debugging ("did my change help, or was it noise?"), audits, rollbacks and handing work to teammates.

Exact bit-for-bit results are hard on GPUs, because some parallel operations add numbers in a varying order and floating-point addition is not associative. Frameworks offer deterministic modes at some cost in speed. A practical goal is often statistical reproducibility: reruns land within a known spread.

Example: two runs of the same fine-tuning job with different seeds score 0.842 and 0.851. Before claiming a new feature's 0.849 is a gain, run several seeds of both versions and compare against that spread.

Habits that help: versioned data, logging the commit and config with every run, and container images for the environment.
concepts.mixup: Setting a random seed is not enough. Changed data, a library upgrade, different hardware or non-deterministic GPU kernels can each change results even with the same seed.

concepts.name: Shadow deployment
concepts.summary: Running a new model on copies of real production requests next to the live model, logging its outputs without ever showing them to users.
concepts.body:
Each live request goes to the current model, whose answer is served, and a copy goes to the candidate, whose answer is only logged. You then compare the two: how often predictions agree, score distributions, latency, error rates and memory use under real load.

It is a safe way to catch problems that offline tests miss, such as training-serving skew, slow responses on real inputs, or crashes on odd requests, with no user impact. The cost is running two models at once.

Its limit is that it cannot measure effects that depend on users acting on the output, such as clicks or sales, because users never see the candidate's answers. For that you need a canary release or an A/B test.

Example: a new fraud model runs in shadow for two weeks. It would have blocked 3% more transactions, and its p99 latency is 40 ms over budget. Both issues are fixed before any customer is affected.
concepts.mixup: In a shadow deployment the candidate serves nobody. In a canary release it serves a small share of real users. Shadow mode tests safety and agreement, while canaries and A/B tests show real user impact.

concepts.name: Canary release
concepts.summary: Rolling out a new model to a small share of real traffic first, watching key metrics, and widening the rollout only while it stays healthy.
concepts.body:
A canary starts with something like 1 to 5% of traffic on the new version. You compare its error rate, latency and model or business metrics with the old version, often through automatic checks. If they hold, traffic steps up, perhaps to 25%, 50% and 100%. If not, traffic goes back to the old version at once.

It limits the blast radius of a bad release: a bug hurts a few users for a short time instead of everyone. It needs the old version kept ready for rollback and metrics that react quickly.

Example: a new ranking model gets 5% of users for a day. Its crash rate is normal, but click-through is 4% lower than the control group's, so it is rolled back before full launch.

Small canary groups give noisy metrics, so a canary is best at catching clear breakage, not at measuring small effects.
concepts.mixup: A canary release is mainly a safety check. An A/B test is a planned experiment with a set sample size, built to measure an effect precisely. They can share traffic-splitting tools, but a canary is not a substitute for a properly powered experiment.

concepts.name: Model monitoring
concepts.summary: Tracking a deployed model's health, inputs, outputs and real-world performance over time, so problems are caught before they cause harm.
concepts.body:
Monitoring covers several layers. Service health: latency, error rate, throughput and cost. Data quality: missing values, schema changes and out-of-range values. Drift: shifts in input features and in prediction scores. Model quality: accuracy, precision, calibration or business metrics, computed once labels arrive. And slices: the same metrics by segment, since an overall average can hide a group that is failing.

Alerts should fire on thresholds that matter, or the team learns to ignore them.

Example: a churn model's overall AUC is stable, but a slice dashboard shows recall for new mobile users fell from 0.70 to 0.45. An app update had renamed an event that fed one feature. A data quality check on that feature would have caught it on day one.

When labels arrive late, input and prediction drift serve as early warnings.
concepts.mixup: Ordinary software monitoring is not enough. A model can return fast, valid responses with no errors while its predictions are quietly wrong. ML monitoring adds data, drift and quality checks on top of service health.

concepts.name: Population stability index
concepts.summary: A drift score that compares how a variable is spread across bins in a reference sample and a recent sample, where larger values mean a bigger shift.
concepts.body:
Bin the variable, often into 10 bins using the deciles of the reference data. For each bin, take the reference share E and the recent share A, then sum over bins:

PSI = Σ (A − E) × ln(A / E)

Every term is zero or positive, so PSI is never negative and is zero only when the shares match. It is also symmetric: swapping the two samples gives the same value. Common rules of thumb are below 0.1 for little change, 0.1 to 0.25 for a moderate shift worth checking, and above 0.25 for a major shift. These cut-offs come from credit scoring practice, not from a statistical test.

Example: one bin held 10% of the training data and now holds 20%. Its term is (0.20 − 0.10) × ln(2) ≈ 0.069. Add the terms for all bins to get the total.

Watch the details: an empty bin makes ln(A / E) undefined, so use a small floor, and results depend on the binning.
concepts.mixup: PSI measures how far a distribution moved, not whether the model got worse. A high PSI on an unimportant feature may not matter, and concept drift can hurt the model while every PSI stays near zero.

concepts.name: Retraining policy
concepts.summary: The rules for when and how a production model is retrained, such as on a fixed schedule, on a drift or performance trigger, or both.
concepts.body:
A policy answers three questions. When: on a schedule such as nightly or weekly, on a trigger such as performance below a threshold, drift above a limit or enough new labels, or both. On what data: a sliding window of recent data, all history, or history with recent data weighted more. How it ships: the new model passes the same checks as any release and must match or beat the live model on a fresh holdout before promotion.

The right cadence depends on how fast the world changes, how long labels take and what training costs. Fraud may need daily retraining, while a stable sensor model may need it yearly.

Example: a demand model retrains weekly on a rolling 12 months of data. It is promoted only if its error on the latest week is no worse than the live model's.

Automatic retraining without these checks can ship a model trained on broken data.
concepts.mixup: Retraining is not always the fix. If performance fell because of a pipeline bug or training-serving skew, retraining on the broken data can make things worse. Find the cause first.

concepts.name: CI/CD for ML
concepts.summary: Automating the testing, validation and release of ML code, data and models, so every change reaches production through the same repeatable checks.
concepts.body:
Normal CI/CD tests code. ML adds two more things that change: data and models. A typical pipeline has unit tests for feature and training code, data validation of schema, ranges and null rates, a training step, quality checks against a fixed evaluation set and against the current production model, checks on latency, size and fairness, and then a staged release such as shadow or canary, with rollback ready.

Many teams add continuous training, where new data triggers the pipeline to retrain and re-validate automatically.

Example: a pull request changes how a feature is bucketed. CI runs the unit tests and retrains a small model on a sample. The quality gate fails because AUC on the fixed evaluation set dropped from 0.91 to 0.88, so the change cannot merge without review.

The aim is that no model reaches users by hand from a notebook.
concepts.mixup: Passing code tests does not mean a model is safe to ship. A pipeline can run cleanly and still produce a worse model. ML pipelines need data and quality gates, not only unit tests.

concepts.name: Batch vs online inference
concepts.summary: Batch inference scores many records on a schedule and stores the results, while online inference computes a prediction on demand when a request arrives.
concepts.body:
Batch inference runs as a job, for example nightly, over a whole table and writes predictions to a store that apps read. It is cheap, simple and efficient at volume, but predictions are only as fresh as the last run, and it scores many records that are never used.

Online inference runs a model behind an API. It can use fresh context, such as what the user just searched, and handles new users or items. It must meet a latency budget, stay available and scale with traffic.

Example: a weekly churn score for 2 million customers suits batch, since retention emails go out once a week. Card payment fraud checks need online inference, because the decision must use the current transaction within tens of milliseconds.

Many systems mix both: precompute heavy parts in batch, such as item embeddings, and do light scoring online at request time.
concepts.mixup: Online inference does not mean the model learns online. It only means predictions are made at request time. Online learning, where the model updates from each new example, is a separate idea.

concepts.name: Label delay
concepts.summary: The gap between when a model makes a prediction and when the true outcome becomes known, which slows down both monitoring and retraining.
concepts.body:
Some labels arrive in seconds, such as a click. Others take weeks or months, such as a loan default, a chargeback or a customer cancelling. Until the label arrives, you cannot measure real accuracy on recent predictions.

This shapes the whole MLOps setup. Quality monitoring lags, so teams watch proxies such as input drift, prediction score distributions and early signals that correlate with the final label. Retraining data always ends some time in the past. And training sets need care, because a recent example with no label yet can be wrongly treated as negative.

Example: fraud chargebacks can take up to 60 days to arrive. A model deployed today gets a reliable precision figure only after about two months. Labelling last week's transactions "not fraud" just because no chargeback has come yet would teach the model that fresh fraud looks legitimate.
concepts.mixup: A missing label on recent data is not a negative label. Treating "not known yet" as "no" biases both training data and metrics. Wait for a maturity window, or model the delay explicitly.

concepts.name: LLM observability
concepts.summary: Capturing traces, inputs, outputs, costs and quality signals from an LLM application in production, so you can debug failures and track quality over time.
concepts.body:
LLM apps fail in ways normal metrics miss: a fluent but wrong answer still returns a success code. Observability adds a trace for each request that records every step: the prompt template and its version, retrieved documents, tool calls, model responses, token counts, latency and cost per step.

On top of traces you run quality checks: automatic evals such as groundedness or format checks, LLM-as-judge scoring on a sample, user feedback such as thumbs up or down, and tracking of refusals and guardrail triggers. Bad traces become new test cases for your evaluation set.

Example: complaints about wrong refund amounts rise. Traces show the retrieval step returns an outdated policy document for 8% of refund questions, and the model faithfully quotes it. The fix is in the index, not the prompt.

Traces often contain personal data, so redact it and set retention limits.
concepts.mixup: Observability is more than logging the final answer. Without the steps in between, such as retrieval and tool calls, you cannot tell whether a bad answer came from the model, the prompt or the context it was given.

concepts.name: Service level objective
concepts.summary: A target for how well a service must perform over a time window, such as 99.9% of requests answered within 300 ms over 30 days.
concepts.body:
Three terms go together. A service level indicator (SLI) is the measurement, such as the share of requests answered within 300 ms. The SLO is the internal target for that SLI over a window. A service level agreement (SLA) is a contract with customers, usually looser than the SLO, with penalties if it is missed.

The gap to 100% is the error budget. A 99.9% availability SLO over a 30-day month allows 0.1% of 43,200 minutes, which is 43.2 minutes of failure. When the budget is used up, teams slow down risky releases and focus on reliability.

For ML services, SLOs often cover latency percentiles, availability and the freshness of features or predictions, and sometimes a quality floor such as a minimum precision on a daily audit.

Example: an LLM assistant sets SLOs of p95 time to first token under 1 second and 99.5% of requests completing without error.
concepts.mixup: An SLO is not an SLA. The SLO is the team's own target, while the SLA is an outside promise with consequences. Latency targets are also set on percentiles, not averages, because averages hide slow requests.

concepts.name: Two-stage recommender
concepts.summary: A recommender design where a fast retrieval stage narrows millions of items to a few hundred candidates and a heavier model ranks those candidates.
concepts.body:
Scoring every item with a rich model on every request is far too slow, so the work is split. Candidate generation, or retrieval, uses cheap methods such as a two-tower model with approximate nearest neighbour search, co-occurrence lists or popular items to pull a few hundred to a few thousand items in milliseconds. Its goal is high recall.

The ranking stage then scores each candidate with a heavier model that can use many features, including crosses of user and item features and live context, to predict clicks, watch time or purchases. Its goal is precision at the top. Many systems add a final re-ranking step for diversity, freshness and business rules.

Example: a video app with 10 million videos retrieves 500 candidates from several sources in 20 ms, ranks them with a gradient-boosted or neural model in 50 ms, then re-ranks the top 50 so no single creator fills the page.
concepts.mixup: The stages are judged differently. Retrieval is judged by recall: did the good items make it into the candidate set? Ranking is judged by order quality, such as NDCG. A great ranker cannot rescue an item that retrieval dropped.

concepts.name: Collaborative filtering
aka: people who bought this also bought
concepts.summary: Recommending items from patterns in many users' behaviour, on the idea that people who agreed in the past will like similar things, without using item content.
concepts.body:
Collaborative filtering works from the user-item interaction matrix of ratings, purchases or clicks. Neighbourhood methods find similar users or similar items, for example by cosine similarity of their interaction vectors. Item-based CF ("people who bought this also bought") is common because item similarities change slowly. Model-based methods, such as matrix factorization, learn a vector for each user and each item so that their dot product predicts the interaction.

Because it needs only behaviour, it can find links that item descriptions would never show.

Example: many viewers of three particular sci-fi films also watch a certain niche documentary. CF recommends that documentary to another viewer of those films, even though nothing in its description mentions sci-fi.

Its weaknesses are cold start, since a new item has no interactions, and a pull toward popular items. Most data is implicit feedback, so a missing interaction does not mean dislike.
concepts.mixup: Collaborative filtering uses who interacted with what. Content-based filtering uses item attributes such as text, genre or price. CF handles new items badly and content-based methods handle them well, which is why hybrid systems are common.

concepts.name: Content-based filtering
concepts.summary: Recommending items whose features resemble what a user liked before, using item attributes such as text, category or embeddings rather than other users' behaviour.
concepts.body:
Each item is described by features: genre, tags, price, or text and image embeddings. A user profile is built from the items they engaged with, for example the average of their embeddings. Candidate items are scored by similarity to that profile, often cosine similarity.

Its strength is that a new item can be recommended as soon as it has features, with no interaction history. It also gives easy explanations ("because you read X") and serves users with niche tastes well.

Its weakness is narrowness. It keeps suggesting more of the same and cannot discover that sci-fi readers also love a certain cookbook. Quality depends on how good the item features are.

Example: a news app embeds every article. A reader who opened three articles about electric cars is shown a new battery-technology article minutes after it is published, before anyone else has clicked it.
concepts.mixup: Content-based filtering solves the new-item cold start, not the new-user one. A user with no history has no profile, so it still needs a fallback such as popular items or a few onboarding questions.

concepts.name: Two-tower model
concepts.summary: A retrieval model where one network embeds the user or query and another embeds items, trained so that matching pairs have a high dot product.
concepts.body:
The query tower takes user features, history or a search query. The item tower takes item features. Both output vectors of the same size, and the score is their dot product or cosine similarity. Training usually uses positive pairs, such as clicks, with in-batch negatives, where the other items in the batch act as non-matches, under a softmax loss.

The key property is that the towers do not interact until the final dot product. So all item embeddings can be computed ahead of time and loaded into an approximate nearest neighbour index. At request time you run only the query tower and search the index, which scales to many millions of items.

Example: a job site embeds 5 million postings each night. When a user opens the app, their tower runs once and the index returns the 300 closest postings in a few milliseconds, which then go to a ranking model.
concepts.mixup: A two-tower model is fast precisely because it cannot model fine interactions between query and item features. A cross-encoder or ranking model sees both together and is more accurate, but too slow for millions of items, so they are used in sequence.

concepts.name: Cold start
concepts.summary: The difficulty of making good predictions for new users or new items that have little or no interaction history.
concepts.body:
Behaviour-based models such as collaborative filtering learn from past interactions, so a brand-new user or item gives them nothing to work with. There are three cases: a new user, a new item and a whole new system.

Common fixes:
- Use content features for new items, such as text or image embeddings.
- Ask new users a few onboarding questions.
- Fall back to popularity in context, such as top items in the user's region.
- Use the signals you do have, such as device, referrer and the first clicks in this session.
- Explore on purpose, for example with a bandit that gives new items some exposure.

Example: a marketplace lists 20,000 new products a day. A pure CF model never shows them, so they never get clicks, so they stay invisible. Giving each new item a small guaranteed share of impressions, placed using its content embedding, breaks that loop.
concepts.mixup: Cold start is not only a new-user problem. New items can be the bigger issue, since a model that never shows them never collects the data to learn about them. The two cases need different fixes.

concepts.name: Learning to rank
concepts.summary: Training a model to order a list of items by relevance for a query or user, optimizing the quality of the ordering rather than each prediction on its own.
concepts.body:
There are three main approaches. Pointwise scores each item alone, such as predicting click probability with ordinary regression or classification. Pairwise learns which of two items should rank higher, with a loss on pairs, as in RankNet. Listwise uses a loss over the whole list, such as a softmax over the list's scores. LambdaMART, a common gradient-boosted ranker, is usually described as pairwise with a listwise target. Its gradients come from pairs, each weighted by how much swapping the two items would change a metric such as NDCG.

Ranking metrics care most about the top positions, which pointwise losses treat like any other. Metric-weighted methods such as LambdaMART put the most effort into the top of the list.

Training data comes from human relevance grades or from clicks, which must be corrected for position bias.

Example: a help-centre search has 50 candidate articles for "reset router password". A pairwise model learns from clicks that the official setup guide should beat an old forum thread, and the list is sorted by its scores.
concepts.mixup: Better pointwise accuracy does not guarantee a better ranking. A model can predict click rates well on average yet order the top few items poorly. Judge ranking models with ranking metrics such as NDCG or MRR.

concepts.name: Position bias
concepts.summary: The tendency of users to click higher-placed results more often just because of where they appear, so clicks overstate how relevant the top positions are.
concepts.body:
Click logs mix two things: whether a user looked at an item and whether they liked it. Items near the top are looked at far more, so a ranker trained naively on clicks learns that whatever it showed first was best, and keeps showing it.

One fix is to estimate how likely each position is to be examined, for example by randomizing the order for a small slice of traffic, then weight each click by the inverse of that probability. Another is to add position as a feature in training and set it to a fixed value at serving time. Interleaving experiments also compare rankers more fairly.

Example: position 1 is examined 90% of the time and position 5 about 30%. A result at position 5 with a 6% click rate may be more relevant than one at position 1 with a 15% click rate, since 6 / 0.30 = 20% versus 15 / 0.90 ≈ 16.7%.
concepts.mixup: A high click rate at the top is not proof of relevance, because it mixes visibility with quality. Position bias is one case of the wider feedback loop, where a model's own choices shape the data it learns from next.

concepts.name: Multi-armed bandit
concepts.summary: A method that repeatedly chooses among options while learning which pays off best, balancing trying uncertain options against using the current best.
concepts.body:
Each option is an arm with an unknown reward, such as a click rate. Each round you pick an arm, see its reward and update your estimates. The tension is exploration versus exploitation. Epsilon-greedy picks the best arm so far most of the time and a random arm with probability ε. Upper confidence bound (UCB) picks the arm with the highest optimistic estimate. Thompson sampling draws a value from each arm's posterior and picks the highest draw. Contextual bandits also use user features, so the choice can differ per person.

Compared with an A/B test, a bandit shifts traffic toward winners while still learning, so less traffic goes to poor options. The price is weaker evidence about how big the differences are.

Example: four headline variants for one article. With ε = 0.1, 90% of readers see the headline with the best click rate so far and 10% see a randomly chosen one, so a slow starter can still catch up.
concepts.mixup: A bandit does not replace every A/B test. A bandit aims to earn the most reward while learning, while an A/B test aims to measure an effect precisely. Bandits suit short-lived choices like headlines, tests suit decisions that need a trustworthy estimate.

concepts.name: Feedback loop
concepts.summary: When a model's predictions change the data it is later trained on, so its own past choices shape, and can distort, what it learns next.
concepts.body:
A recommender shows items, users click among what they were shown, and those clicks become training data. Items the model favours get more exposure and more clicks, which convinces it they are even better. Items it never shows collect no evidence. Over time diversity shrinks and errors reinforce themselves.

It appears outside recommenders too. A fraud model blocks transactions, so you never learn whether the blocked ones were really fraud. Predictive policing sends officers where the model expects crime, which records more crime there.

Ways to break the loop: keep a small random or exploration slice of traffic, log what was shown and its probability of being shown so training can correct for it, monitor diversity and catalogue coverage, and collect labels for a sample of cases the model rejected.

Example: after a music app launches a ranker trained on clicks, the top 1% of songs grow from 30% to 55% of all plays in six months, while plays of new artists fall.
concepts.mixup: A feedback loop is not ordinary data drift. Drift comes from the world changing on its own. A feedback loop comes from the model changing its own training data, so simply retraining on the new data tends to deepen it.

concepts.name: Capacity estimation
concepts.summary: Rough calculations of the traffic, compute, memory and storage a system will need, used to size hardware and spot bottlenecks before building.
concepts.body:
Start from users and their behaviour, convert to requests per second, then to resources. Average QPS = daily requests / 86,400. Plan for the peak, which as a rule of thumb is often 2 to 5 times the average, then add headroom. Divide by what one server or GPU can handle, using throughput measured at your latency target.

For LLMs, estimate tokens, not just requests: QPS × (input + output tokens), plus memory for weights and the KV cache.

Example: 10 million daily users each send 5 requests, so 50 million requests a day, about 580 QPS on average. With a peak of 3 times, that is about 1,740 QPS. If one GPU replica handles 60 QPS within the latency target, you need 1,740 / 60 = 29 replicas, then a few more for redundancy, say 35.

Storage works the same way: 50 million logged requests at 2 KB each is 100 GB per day.

Write down every assumption. Interviewers care more about clear, checkable steps than exact numbers.
concepts.mixup: Sizing for average load is a classic mistake. Peaks and bursts decide how much capacity you need, and running servers close to 100% utilization makes queueing delay, and so latency, rise sharply.

concepts.name: Latency budget
concepts.summary: The total response time a request is allowed, split into a share for each step, so every component knows how much time it may spend.
concepts.body:
Start from the product target, usually a percentile such as p99 under 200 ms, then divide it along the request path: network, feature lookups, retrieval, model inference and post-processing, plus a margin for spikes. Each team designs to its share.

The budget drives design choices: which features can be fetched live, how big the ranking model can be, how many candidates to score, what to cache and which steps can run in parallel. Steps in sequence add up, while parallel steps cost only as much as the slowest one.

Example: a search page has 200 ms at p99. Network and API overhead take 30 ms, query understanding 15 ms, retrieval 40 ms, ranking 80 ms and rendering 15 ms, leaving a 20 ms margin. Adding a 60 ms reranker means something else must shrink or run in parallel.

When one request fans out to many services, it waits for the slowest, so each part's tail latency matters a lot.
concepts.mixup: Meeting the budget on average does not mean meeting it. Budgets are set on tail percentiles, because users notice slow requests and fan-out calls wait for their slowest part. Also, adding each step's p99 usually overstates the end-to-end p99, so treat that sum as a safe upper estimate.

concepts.name: Model cascade
concepts.summary: A chain of models from cheap to expensive, where each request is answered by the cheapest model that is confident enough and only hard cases move on.
concepts.body:
The first model handles the request and gives a confidence, such as a calibrated probability or a verifier's judgement. If the confidence clears a threshold, its answer is used. If not, the request passes to the next, stronger model. Simple rules can sit at the front to settle the easiest cases.

It cuts average cost and latency while keeping quality close to the strongest model, as long as the confidence signal is reliable. Thresholds are tuned on held-out data to hit a quality target.

Example: a support classifier answers 80% of tickets with confidence above 0.9. The other 20% go to a large LLM. If the small model costs 1 unit and the large one 20, every ticket pays 1 and a fifth also pay 20, so the average is 1 + 0.2 × 20 = 5 units, against 20 for sending everything to the large model.

Escalated requests are slower, since they run both models.
concepts.mixup: A cascade tries models in order and escalates on low confidence. A router predicts up front which model to call, so each request runs only one model. Cascades depend on calibrated confidence, since an overconfident first model never escalates its own mistakes.
